speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We then appointed the ElderShield Review Committee in October that year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Committee engaged widely and deliberated rigorously on how to enhance ElderShield and strengthen support for long-term care financing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Committee’s Chairman Mr Chaly Mah and some of his Committee members are with us today in the Chamber.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I would also like to thank all Singaporeans who contributed their views and suggestions during the process.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: CareShield Life will offer better protection and greater assurance for Singaporeans’ long-term care needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It is a significant step in strengthening our social safety net.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It is part of our overall strategy to prepare for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have around five working adults to each Singaporean above 65 today, but by 2030, this ratio will fall to 2.7.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our rising life expectancy and falling mortality rates are positive developments.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But living longer also means that we face higher risks of frailty in our old age.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Some of us may require long-term care and assistance with daily living activities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is why we had started investing and preparing years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We rolled out Healthcare 2020 in 2012, which included building long-term care and aged care facilities, improving the quality of these services and keeping them affordable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We then went Beyond Healthcare 2020, to ensure that we can meet our long-term healthcare needs in a sustainable manner.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We want to go Beyond Hospital to the Community, by investing in community care and bringing social and healthcare services closer to our people.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are moving Beyond Quality to Value by spurring productivity improvement and providing better guidance on cost-effective treatment.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We are moving Beyond Healthcare to Health by encouraging Singaporeans to lead healthier lives.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have also made several enhancements to better support our seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We implemented MediShield Life in 2015 to provide universal coverage with better protection for all, for life, especially the seniors; we also introduced the Pioneer Generation (PG) Package to give our Pioneers greater peace of mind; we have been developing eldercare facilities and services, as well as strengthening support for the care of our elderly in our homes and in the community; we are also integrating health and social care better, and expanding the Community Network for Seniors; we have been growing and developing the long-term care workforce through recruitment, training and productivity improvement so that we are ready for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: And this will continue to grow as our population ages.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The next step is to ensure that our long-term care financing system is strengthened to complement our efforts to develop eldercare services and support.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: How should we finance our long-term care needs in a way that keeps costs affordable, yet sustainable for future generations to come?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There are four key principles we need to bear in mind when we design our long-term care financing system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It should help those who need long-term care to afford basic and essential care, by tapping on the various sources of financing that are available, including Government and community support, personal and family savings, risk-pooling through insurance, and additional safety nets to prevent people from falling through the cracks.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Long-term care needs of our seniors are by nature very diverse.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, the financing system should be flexible and enable individuals to use services most appropriate for their care needs and circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Whether care is provided at home or by day care centres or nursing homes, and whether it is provided by formal caregivers or by family members, our financing system must have the flexibility to support these options.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: All Singaporeans, regardless of their income or health status, should be well-supported by our overall long-term care financing scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: They should be assured that our system will help them with their long-term care when they need it, be it from insurance, savings or subsidies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Long-term care needs run far into the future with significant uncertainties.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We have to ensure that our system is sustainable over the long-term and that we will have sufficient funds to meet the needs in the future when they occur.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We should avoid passing the burden to future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: These three components work together to achieve our principles of affordability, flexibility, inclusiveness and sustainability.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will expand the role of insurance in our long-term care financing system, with the introduction of the new CareShield Life scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In this regard, I would like to thank Ms Sylvia Lim, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, Mr Leon Perera and Mr Dennis Tan, for allowing us to address your Parliamentary Questions (PQs) at this debate.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: I would also like to thank Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Ms Chia Yong Yong for your earlier PQs, which you have withdrawn after we informed you that we would be tabling a Motion on CareShield Life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Our long-term care needs and how much we need to save individually are difficult to predict with great accuracy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Some are surprised by our “one-in-two” statistic and asked why is it that we do not see half of the seniors being severely disabled.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: If you look around the House, some of us are above 65, but we do not look severely disabled.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The simple reason is that we do not all become severely disabled all at the same time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: So, it actually happens across a period of time, through our lifespan, and generally after 65.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There is also uncertainty in the duration a person remains severely disabled.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: If we save for four years of disability, but remain disabled for 10 years, we would not have saved enough.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: On the other hand, if we saved for 10 years, but we have been disabled for less, we would have over-saved, and therefore, insurance plays a role.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Insurance allows each cohort of Singaporeans to pool our risks together to support the long-term care needs of that cohort in a more efficient way.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: There are two broad approaches to financing long-term care insurance across the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The first is a pay-as-you-go system, where funds collected in a particular year, often through taxes, are used to pay for the claims for that year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: That is why you pay as you go.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This means that the younger working population will most likely be funding the claims made mostly by the seniors, and most of the seniors have stopped working.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This approach creates significant intergenerational transfers, where the younger cohorts pay for the needs of the older cohorts.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is not sustainable, especially for an ageing population, where the number of seniors is growing at a much faster pace than that of the younger working population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The second approach is one where each cohort pays for its own needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is done by putting aside funding while one is still working, and pays for the long-term care needs later, usually after one has retired.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Insurance like ElderShield and CareShield Life are such pre-funded schemes, not pay-as-you-go schemes.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This approach minimises intergenerational transfers and avoids passing the burden to future generations and helps to keep the scheme sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Senior Minister of State Chee Hong Tat will elaborate further later on.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Pre-funded insurance schemes like ElderShield and CareShield Life allow us to prepare for our long-term care needs in a sustainable way, while risk pooling allows us to average out the risk and funds among us so that we need not worry about over-saving and yet have the assurance that, should the worst happen, we will have sufficient funds.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: CareShield Life will be more than an insurance scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It will become an integral part of our social safety net.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: It will provide better protection and assurance for all Singaporeans who join the scheme, through higher payouts for life for Singaporeans who are severely disabled and for life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We welcome and support the Committee’s recommendation for universal coverage for future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is an important step forward as it would ensure basic protection for the long-term care needs of our future generations, regardless of their health, disability or financial status.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: This is in line with our vision of inclusivity as it allows those with pre-existing disability to be covered and also ensures that no one will drop out because they are unable to pay the premiums.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Preparing for our old-age needs is often of low priority when we are young, as we tend to focus more on building our career and bringing up our children, and this is understandable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But starting to prepare only when we are old would be very challenging.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Therefore, having a universal long-term care insurance scheme for future cohorts is critical and will ensure that our future generations will have a basic level of protection.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: The Government will also do our part in supporting this national initiative.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: In 2020, we will enrol those who are born between 1980 and 1990.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: After that, future cohorts of Singapore residents will be enrolled when they reach the age of 30.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: We will be rolling out CareShield Life for existing cohorts in 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Existing cohorts are those who are born in 1979 or earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: As recommended by the Review Committee, CareShield Life will be optional for them, because of their diverse circumstances.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Some of them may already be severely disabled.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Some may have made their own plans for their long-term care needs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: Some of them may also face significantly higher annual premiums, especially for the older generations, as they have fewer years to spread their premium payments over.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: But because CareShield Life will provide better protection and assurance, we will encourage as many as possible of the existing cohort members to join the scheme if they are not severely disabled.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: To do this, we will provide significant support for existing cohorts to join CareShield Life.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Gan Kim Yong)
text: First, to help lower- and middle-income Singaporeans with their premiums, we will provide similar means-tested premium subsidies as future cohorts of up to 30%.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The example is one Mr Tan, who is 42 years old.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To join CareShield Life, his starting annual premium in 2021 would be about $380, after taking into account the premiums he had already paid under ElderShield.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: He no longer needs to pay the ElderShield premiums once he switches over to CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: However, as he is low-income, he will receive a 30% subsidy on his premiums.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is on the assumption of an increase of 2% a year for the remaining part of his CareShield Life participation.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: An older policyholder, who is covered on ElderShield 300, would need to pay an additional catch-up component for 10 years, as he would not have paid as much premiums as those insured under ElderShield 400.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And, for someone who is currently uninsured, his catch-up component would be higher as he has not paid any premium at all.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As recommended by the Review Committee, CareShield Life will be administered by the Government on a not-for-profit basis.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Government will set up an insurance fund which will be ringfenced for CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The fund will be administered by the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: And all premiums collected and any returns from investments will remain entirely within the fund and used solely for the benefit of policyholders.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The fund will be audited annually to ensure that all the monies are accounted for.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Government will also set up an independent Council to provide advice on the administration of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The Council will also regularly review CareShield Life and the recommended premiums and payout adjustments to the Government, in accordance with an actuarially sound adjustment framework.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While CareShield Life will provide better assurance for our future cohorts, we recognise that not everyone will be able to join CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: For example, those in existing cohorts who are already severely disabled will not be able to join the scheme.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Those who are healthy but very old also have fewer years to spread their premium payments compared to the younger ones, so they may also find the annual premiums a high hurdle.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: At the same time, some of those who join CareShield Life may require additional support, depending on their care needs and financial resources.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will, therefore, strengthen two other parts of our long-term care financing system – savings and subsidies – that will help to provide better assurance and support for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, we will enable Singaporeans to tap on their personal and spouse’s MediSave savings for long-term care needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Today, Singaporeans can use their MediSave to pay for ElderShield premiums and, in time to come, CareShield Life premiums.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We can also allow MediSave to be used for long-term care expenses, just like we allow it to be used for medical expenses.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Given the diverse needs of long-term care, withdrawals will be in cash so that there is more flexibility on how to use the money, including on home and community care or residential care.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Withdrawals can be up to $200 per month, depending on the balance in the respective MediSave accounts.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is to ensure there are some savings to provide for other healthcare needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Second, just like we have MediFund for medical services, we will set up a new ElderFund scheme in 2020, to support Singaporeans from low-income households who are severely disabled.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Eligible Singapore Citizens can receive up to $250 per month in cash, for as long as they are severely disabled.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There will be no cap on the payout duration for ElderFund payouts.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The scheme will benefit those who may not be able to join CareShield Life, such as those among the existing cohorts who may already be severely disabled before the launch of CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: It will also provide additional support for Singaporeans with low MediSave balances and savings to meet their long-term care needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The three enhancements, taken together – CareShield Life, use of MediSave for long-term care, and ElderFund – will provide all Singaporeans with better protection and assurance for their long-term care needs, for life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The payouts from these schemes should not be viewed in isolation, but as part of our overall long-term care financing framework.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These schemes will also work with existing social safety net, including Government subsidies and assistance schemes, such as MediFund and ComCare, community support, and personal savings and family support, to help Singaporeans in need.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This reflects our key social objective of forging an inclusive society where society, individuals and their families, as well as the Government, come together to support the long-term care needs of our ageing society through insurance, savings and Government assistance.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We are launching a package of enhancements to long-term care financing so as to better prepare Singaporeans for our future long-term care needs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will be reaching out to Singaporeans over the next few years.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But I would submit that many of us may take our mobility and individual independence for granted even more so.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This morning, many of us would have gotten out of bed, had our breakfast, dressed ourselves, maybe even gone in to have shower, did some toileting, but we do not often give these actions a second thought.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But we can lose all of these and become disabled and dependent, sometimes suddenly, catastrophically, such as after a stroke.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My late grandmother was 70 years old and she was one of the most active individuals I have ever met.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She was still working and she would always walk instead of taking the bus.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One afternoon, after an afternoon nap, she found that she could no longer do any of these things.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: She could not walk by herself, she could not take a bus, she could not feed herself or even go to the toilet by herself.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And this was all in a matter of a few seconds.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Or it could happen after a terrible accident, such as with a spinal cord injury.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Sometimes, the disability may come slowly, insidiously, such as with chronic nerve or muscle diseases and sometimes through mental problems, such as dementia.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In January this year, the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Health submitted its recommendations on enhancing ElderShield to the Ministry of Health (MOH), and we note that our recommendations are broadly in line with those made by the ElderShield Review Committee.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One, Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong described ElderShield as the “one remaining piece” that is needed to consolidate the progressive enhancements to our social safety net.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, the GPC believes that in order for it to fulfil its function as a cornerstone of our social security apparatus, ElderShield coverage for our population should be universal.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Two, as for any social welfare programme, a careful balance has to be struck between increasing and expanding benefits so that the programme remains relevant and useful, and yet keeping the scheme both affordable and sustainable for the long term.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Three, if ElderShield is to be universal with mandatory enrolment, then the GPC believes that the Government will have to provide targeted financial assistance to ensure that all Singaporeans will be able to participate in this social security programme, which is designed to increase peace of mind in the event of severe disability.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Could the Minister elaborate on the mechanism through which payouts and premiums are determined and adjusted to ensure that the system remains fiscally relevant yet affordable for all Singaporeans?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For instance, when will we know that $600 a month is no longer adequate, and how much should the minimum payout be revised to?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note also that Singaporean women tend to have lower average MediSave balances than men, so I hope that consideration be given to provide additional premium support for women as well.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Three, I hope that the Government will remain focused on investing or continuing to invest in Intermediate and Long-Term Care (ILTC) infrastructure and manpower and focus on keeping such services affordable.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: CareShield Life is a means of financing ILTC for the severely and permanently disabled, but such services are also necessary for those who are less severely disabled, or thankfully only temporarily disabled.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If we do not keep ILTC costs in check, then payouts will be unable to keep up, and CareShield Life will become ineffective.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope the Ministry will also share with this House how it intends to keep ILTC costs affordable for all, and also the support care within the community.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that, as with the rollout of MediShield Life and the PG Package, the Government will have a comprehensive communications plan to help Singaporeans understand the scheme better.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I believe there have been cases in the past where ElderShield policyholders who are able to actually make claims when they became disabled, have not done so because they were simply not aware that they could do so, or even that they were on the scheme.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For those who are already disabled but cannot be covered by CareShield Life, I am sure the Government will continue to provide the necessary assistance and support to them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is unlike hospitalisation for emergencies or acute conditions requiring a person to be in the hospital for a relatively short period of time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Once the acute stage has passed, a person usually requires some step-down care for a number of years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This can be unaffordable to families, necessitating a broad-based financial support scheme.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, I agree that ElderShield, in its current form, is not adequate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With this strict qualification criteria, the persons eligible to make ElderShield claims are those who face significant costs of treatment, care and medications.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The current payouts of $300 to $400 per month are too small to give families the peace of mind they need.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today’s debate is important, as CareShield Life is an opportunity to demonstrate our values.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As we battle inequality and disturbing signs of an economic class divide, new policies for risk-pooling and mutual support will be increasingly necessary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this regard, it is comforting to read in the ElderShield Review Committee’s Report that a respondent told the Committee that he did not mind paying more premiums as “we are all a society”.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, there are certain aspects of the proposed scheme that appear to us to be more controversial.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, for a compulsory scheme, have the premiums been set too high, based on assumptions that are debatable?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To ensure greater confidence and buy-in to the scheme, how transparent will the process of setting premiums and payouts be?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These and other issues will be covered by my other colleagues.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For my part, I shall focus on two aspects of particular concern: first, the eligibility criteria for claims, that is, how disabled must a person be before being able to make a claim?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, how disabled must a person be to make a claim?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To justify such a national draw of MediSave savings, CareShield Life must be meaningful.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: CareShield Life must kick in to provide financial support to our citizens in times of disability.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the current proposal, CareShield will adopt the same eligibility criteria used in ElderShield.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The assessors will have to determine whether a potential claimant is disabled enough as to not be able to do at least three of the six ADLs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Here I wish to share the experience of one of my residents, who has since passed away.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This resident, Mr K, was suffering from an advanced stage of kidney failure and already had his leg amputated earlier due to diabetes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The insurer later decided to discontinue Mr K’s ElderShield benefits as the insurer’s panel doctor had assessed that he could perform all of the six ADLs “although partially”.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When I appealed on his behalf for a re-assessment, the insurer wrote back to him to fill up another claim form.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When I saw him there, he requested me to write to the insurer to say that he would not be filling up the form as he was in the hospice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Eventually, his daughter filled up the form, and I understand that the hospice doctors assisted to get his ElderShield benefits restored.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When I read about the ElderShield premiums in the billions that have been collected over the years, it struck me how Mr K and his family have apparently been abandoned in their time of need.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is the experience of Mr K an aberration?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If this is going to be the experience that will be carried over to CareShield Life, it would be unacceptable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By the time a person is unable to do three ADLs, one is in dire straits.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One is either headed towards a nursing home or needs someone to provide care full-time.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Before one reaches this stage, if CareShield can give some payouts, then it is likely that the disabled person can continue to be looked after at home with some part-time help.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The payouts will fulfil a very important gap to enable the disabled person to age in place and not tie up another nursing home bed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is CareShield not a good time to review the three-ADL test?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Why not use a test of inability to perform two ADLs instead?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I note from Annex B of the Committee’s Report that under the long-term care scheme in Germany, persons can claim if they are assessed to have at least some impairment to independence on physical and mental conditions, with payouts which are tiered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this regard, if a two-ADL test or some more flexible disability test is adopted for CareShield Life payouts, then more of the older cohorts currently on ElderShield may also be incentivised to join CareShield.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With this looming fact in mind, CareShield must have meaningful coverage, and my view is that the “three ADLs test” needs to be reviewed and readjusted to serve this end.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Yet, the Committee insists that CareShield Life’s features are “universality” and “risk-pooling”.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Government clarify whether there is any other country with compulsory long-term care insurance that discriminates premiums by gender?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In any case, Mr Speaker, it is up to the Government to decide whether this recommendation of the Committee should be adopted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Committee writes that having gender-differentiated premiums is needed to ensure that CareShield Life “remains sustainable regardless of the mix of men and women who join”.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But for a compulsory scheme, where every birth cohort will be included, does this argument, of not knowing the mix of men and women who will join, hold water?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I refer to a 2010 article by Nicholas Barr, Professor at the London School of Economics, entitled “Long-Term Care: A Suitable Case for Social Insurance”.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Prof Barr agrees that to finance long-term care needs, using compulsory social insurance rather than optional private insurance will better cushion citizens from risk and uncertainty.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In addition, we must also recognise the fact that many women give up their careers and personal ambitions to do unpaid caregiving for their families, services which the families would otherwise have to pay for.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A 2017 report by the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) found that women are much more likely than men to remain outside the labour force for family-related responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The younger women between 30 and 39 years old cited childcare as the main reason for not working, while females aged 60 and above cited housework and caregiving responsibilities as the main reason for not working.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Married women often provide care for their husbands, delaying or even preventing the men’s progression to becoming disabled.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When husbands need long-term care, wives are there.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Daughters, and daughters-in-law, too, often step up to the plate.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: By so doing, many women have lower CPF balances than men.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It seems that the opportunity costs to women are being repaid by higher premiums for CareShield!

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If we talk about risk-pooling within each generation, with each generation paying for itself, is it too much to ask to risk-pool between the genders and use unisex tables for premiums?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The CareShield Life proposal has much potential to be a strong social safety net for our people.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is a great opportunity which should not be squandered.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: That has caused some of us to wonder about whether the Government had sufficient time to deliberate on the report.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And I thought, as a preliminary point, the Minister may wish to clarify that.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I am also, therefore, glad that Minister has moved this debate to allow Members to seek clarifications for which I have also many.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: It is, nonetheless, in many ways, an improvement over ElderShield.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister has explained the rationale for the exclusion of certain Singaporeans, but I hope that we can continue to consider the ways in which we can provide assistance in a more equitable and comforting manner.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And what is the treatment for persons who have medical conditions but no disability?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In respect of the Government schemes that the Minister has raised which will be used to support those who are not covered under either ElderShield or CareShield Life, I would like to know whether there would be a single set of eligibility criteria.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Will there also be simplified applications and administration in those schemes to facilitate access to the assistance?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: From the administrator's perspectives, each would have their accountability for the administration of a scheme, but from the users' perspectives, we are all only seeking one single route of assistance.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Also, ultimately, for clarity, could the Ministry clarify which groups of Singaporeans will have no protection under ElderShield, CareShield and no assistance under Government schemes?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I think it is important for us to know who we are and what we can do for them.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: So, it is very good that we understand who qualifies; it is important for us to know who does not.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Also, with respect to the conversion of protection from ElderShield to CareShield, I have noted that premiums paid under ElderShield will be taken into account for the payment of premiums under CareShield, as the Minister has said.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But I wonder if the Ministry can also give more clarifications and examples of how such consideration would be applied.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: In relation to excess premiums collected under ElderShield, since Eldershield is an opt-out scheme that came into operation by the compulsion of the state, I would submit that although insurance policies are issued separately by insurers to the insured, actually there is really no direct contractual relationship between the insured and the insurance company.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Because this is a compulsory scheme – we either opt out, or we are in; we have no way to negotiate; we cannot even choose our insurers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, they are, I submit, the agents of the state.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: That being so, the premiums that they collect – the excess premiums they collect – does the state have a claim?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I am prepared to concede that the profits that they make out of those premiums should be retained by them, but perhaps the Minister can clarify how the excess premiums will be treated when CareShield is launched.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I have raised what basically relates to actuarial consideration applicable under ElderShield, and I believe that this will also carry through to the considerations under CareShield Life as well.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister perhaps further clarify also actuarial considerations for the exclusion of persons with pre-existing conditions for conversion from ElderShield to CareShield, and for the exclusion of persons with pre-existing medical conditions who were born before 1980?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I know we are all excluded, but could it be argued that there could be an element of discrimination?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps the Minister may wish to consider from that perspective.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And in light of the Committee’s recommendation that premiums should be actuarially priced and adjusted regularly to take into account changes in payout quantum and claims experience, we accept that proper premium quantum may be difficult to assess in light of significant uncertainties.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: And a few final questions to the Minister for clarification.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that CareShield is an important part of this big piece of puzzle that we are trying to build.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: But other than putting pieces together, can there be synergies to be built among the assistance schemes of ElderShield, CareShield, MediShield, MediFund, rather than just taking a defensive approach – a stopping-the-gap approach?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Are there positive synergies that can be achieved out of that?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The final question is probably the easiest, which is on the administration of the scheme.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Subject to my clarifications, Sir, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Making CareShield compulsory and universal and separately collecting premiums earlier from the age of 30, represents a fundamental reshaping of Singapore's long-term care insurance scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the outset, it is important that the Government not underestimate the extent of misinformation surrounding the scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The recent WhatsApp messages which the Government sought to debunk through the mainstream media about it allegedly profiting from CareShield Life can be put down to some perceived pain points and public education gaps.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Many of these find their roots in the lack of knowledge about the principles behind long-term care schemes, such as ElderShield, but also in the use of statistics and data that are based on projections for which little detail and clarification have been provided thus far.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In particular, the question of ever-escalating premiums after transitional subsidies and CareShield Life's likely loss ratio, given the ElderShield experience, has created considerable unease in the public mind.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While the use of MediSave to pay CareShield premiums was recommended by the Committee, this has also raised the prospect of a further depletion of CPF members' MediSave account towards another compulsory scheme after the recently announced MediShield Life, a scheme whose transitional subsidies are only going to be phased out in 2019.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the case of CareShield Life, the effect of technological disruptions on permanent jobs, the gig economy and more contract jobs in the workplace creates insecurities which impact sustained participation in compulsory schemes, particularly when future premiums are going to increase.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From footnote 10 in the Committee’s report, this is an MOH estimate based on local data, supplemented by international data.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This factoid, which appears prominently in the Executive Summary of the Committee’s Report, has raised eyebrows leading some to enquire whether it is unrealistically dire, legitimising higher and earlier premium payments.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would like the Minister to explain this projection, specifically, how the Ministry came to this conclusion, because many Singaporeans cannot visualise how it coheres with the reality they see around them today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More details on this statistic would be welcome.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This, in turn, has led some to focus narrowly on the by now familiar statistic that ElderShield collected about $2.6 billion in premiums while paying out only slightly in excess of $100 million from 2002 to 2016.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fairness to ElderShield, this point cannot be intuitively understood until one appreciates that ElderShield continues to provide lifetime coverage after one stops paying premiums and the scheme requires significant pre-funding to anticipate sufficient payouts for policyholders.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, it would be important to reveal the actuarial principles and considerations behind both ElderShield and CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this regard, there are some questions I seek the Minister to shed light on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When ElderShield was launched in 2002, MOH made a specific provision in its ElderShield contract with the private insurers to return up to 50% of any accumulated surplus to existing policyholders, if the actual claims experience should turn out to be different from what was projected in 2002.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the first five years of the scheme, ElderShield claims have been lower than those projected in 2002.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On what basis, did the Ministry set the rebate quantum at 50% when ElderShield was first introduced, and is there a rebate quantum assigned for CareShield Life and, if so, what is it, or is this a matter for the Independent Council to pursue?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How often will actuarial principles be reviewed, a point that becomes very significant, particularly for those who may have passed away but contributed significantly by way of premiums in the past?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, the Committee's report calls for the setting up of an Independent Council and calls on its recommendations to be made public.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would argue that it is in the Government’s interest to consider if it could go further before the CareShield Life Bill is introduced next year.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are good reasons for the Government to consider taking such an approach.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, such a commitment to openness would go hand-in-hand with CareShield Life’s universal and inclusive approach based on risk-pooling which makes every Singaporean in each cohort, his brother and sister’s keeper.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As all Singaporeans contribute to the risk pool, it follows that the Government should make it easier for Singaporeans to take ownership of the schemes they are enrolled into and make enquiries on any aspect of the scheme’s administration.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In all likelihood, more questions, not fewer ones, on future and previous long-term care projections will be raised, complete with misgivings, apprehensions and inaccuracies in the coffee shops and on social media.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A proactive approach to public education would minimise this prospect and an open information regime would go a long way to addressing criticisms pertaining to transparency and accountability.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, the administration of CareShield Life presents an opportunity to pilot a fresh approach towards public education of Government policies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even as some intentionally perpetuate misinformation about policy, there are yet many others who have genuine enquiries on various aspects of CareShield Life that they may be unsure about.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A Freedom of Information regime with respect to CareShield Life can promote the Committee’s recommendation to better educate the public about the scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More importantly, the advantage of such an approach towards education is that the public discourse is less likely to be antagonistic but more data- and fact-driven.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It will mean men will pay more and women less.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Motion gives Parliament scope to rethink the concept of inclusivity for long-term care and define it to mean that men and women will not be treated differently.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans will need peace of mind to be certain that their healthcare needs are taken care of, especially their long-term care needs as people live longer.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Healthcare for the elderly has been a main worry not only to the elderly but also to the young, as they shoulder the burden of care for their loved ones in their old age when their parents require long-term care.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With smaller family size and low fertility rate, the issue of eldercare has become increasingly pertinent.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Is it the state, the family or the individual?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is, indeed, a collective effort of everyone.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If we truly call ourselves to be an inclusive nation, we must partake in our social responsibility, be it in the form of insurance or risk-pooling.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: These three areas are critical and help ensure that the proposed scheme is sustainable to meet the long-term care needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The scheme does not only benefit Singaporeans who require long-term care, but also their caregivers, to cushion their financial burden on taking care of them.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For this scheme to be effective, the proposed payouts need to be reviewed periodically to reflect the cost of living in Singapore, especially the healthcare cost.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How often will the Government review the adequacy of this payout?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This certainly arises in the minds of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Specifically, the amount should at least defray a significant portion of their expenses, transportation cost and caregiver costs, notwithstanding consumables and drugs.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Is there any benchmark set to defray certain percentage of the cost of long-term care?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: While we look at the social safety net for their long-term care need, we also must ensure that our healthcare cost is sustainable.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The fear is, will the spiralling healthcare cost lead to escalating premium and cash outlay by Singaporeans?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: All efforts to contain healthcare cost must run in tandem with such insurance schemes.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On Recommendation 9, I support the call for the Government to administer an enhanced scheme.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We do not want a similar state of affairs like in the past where the Integrated Shield Plan (IP) with no claim limit was sold as a sweetener to entice many Singaporeans, including the mature and older ones, at a very high premium with increasing age.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Cost of medical bills become exorbitant with the full insurance coverage under the IP.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Healthcare cost needs to be curbed for greater sustainability.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: To strengthen transparency, the Government should have additional safeguards and periodic reviews of how these monies are utilised, especially when these monies are invested in varying investment portfolios.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If CPF Board were to administer the scheme in addition to the other schemes, that is MediShield Life, CPF LIFE and so on, will there be additional safeguards and constant reviews of how these monies are used, especially when we recognise the fact that any investments have potential risk to it?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What is the tolerance limit to risk and losses?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will the principle of perhaps an assurance of net gain over a time horizon, for example, five years, be adopted since it is understandable that there is bound to be risks, that is losses and gains, for any investments?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What are the safeguards in place and are there adequate controls, accountability and transparency?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is also equally important to invest in public education and awareness since the enhanced scheme is new and relatively complex.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It should be communicated in simple terms to the lay person.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is particularly relevant to the millennial since there was no option given for them to opt out of this scheme.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: So, accountability and effective communication of the policy will lead to better appreciation of the scheme and help ease unhappiness from the lack of choice.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: On the technicalities of CareShield Life, I wish to seek some clarifications: according to page 63 of the White Paper on the ESRC Report, it states that the impact of cognitive impairments on functional ability should be explicitly considered in the disability assessment framework for claims.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How will mental health issues and cognitive impairments be factored into disability assessments for CareShield Life?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Mental health issues and cognitive impairments in older Singaporeans do affect their ability to perform ADLs and are significant issues that will be faced by the growing segment of our ageing population.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The assessment should ideally be at no cost at all.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Government look into either reducing the difference in premiums, or provide greater financial support, so that women are not doubly-penalised in having to pay for higher premiums, especially for those with lower income?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What kind of additional coverage is being considered besides the long-term care fund, such as ElderFund, and withdrawal of cash from MediSave?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Government review and consider for a second wave of PG Package for those who missed out on the last wave?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Healthcare needs are major concerns of our older citizens.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We need to look after their needs adequately.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We also need to start educating Singaporeans to sign up for Lasting Power of Attorney to undertake decisions on behalf of them.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: All things must run in tandem to ensure an affordable, accessible and holistic healthcare for Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I feel that with CareShield Life in place, our Government has completed the provision of the basic safety net for long-term care for all Singaporeans, especially with regard to their healthcare.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is taken together with the implementation of MediShield Life, as well as with our existing MediSave and MediFund schemes.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This will give many Singaporeans peace of mind on their healthcare and long-term care needs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I first spoke on ElderShield in May 2002, several months before its implementation.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, this is the 12th time I am speaking in this House on this topic.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Before its implementation in 2002, I already raised the concern over its inadequacy in its payout of $300 and in its tenure of payment of five years.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This payout was upgraded with another $400-version subsequently.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Those individuals with three out of six ADLs, which are washing, dressing, feeding, going to toilet, walking and transferring, such as moving from a bed to chair and vice versa, are totally dependent on others for their daily living.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, Minister Gan Kim Yong himself asked in this House, in this Chamber in 2002, on the reasons for citizens opting out of ElderShield at the time, whether it was because of the $300 payout or because of the difficulty in qualifying for the payout with three ADLs.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Moreover, this amount will remain flat without adjustments to inflation after start of claim.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In the context of Singapore, with increasing smaller families and dual-income families, caring for the severely disabled family members at home is usually with the help of domestic helpers.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The payout of $600 will be inadequate for this domestic help, let alone paying for other hefty expenses, such as medical equipment, higher medical costs, physiotherapy and so on.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The latter are usually required by the severely disabled individuals.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Whilst I understand that keeping the premium of the CareShield Life affordable is necessary, the adequacy and usefulness of CareShield Life are just as important.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: In this context, I feel that three out of six ADLs for payout are too onerous, two ADLs criteria would have been a better proposition.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The reason is that those with just two ADLs alone, like inability to feed or to go to the toilet, will already need full-time assistance.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Even the loss of just one ADL can already make significant impacts on one's life in mobility and in income.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: My concern is that with lesser CareShield Life, for those with two ADLs, their families may take the option of sending their dependent family members to community hospitals or letting them overstay in acute hospitals, resulting in higher burdens in the end for the families and for the Government.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This is a better option than going to private insurers that will never be like the not-for-profit Government policy proclaimed for CareShield Life.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Presently, ElderShield has a relatively low claims-to-premiums ratio outcome.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The number of claimants last year was in the region of 1,750.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Considering the disability prevalence rate presently of about 5% for those 65 years and above, it means that there are already some 15,000 people requiring aged-care facility per year.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could the Minister give an explanation for the low number of claimants?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Is the main reason being the three ADLs' eligibility as too onerous?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Could it also be that the claiming process had been made difficult?

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many people had lamented that they forgot to claim ElderShield.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: For those who tried to claim ElderShield, the process was daunting in filling up forms and looking for assessors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: There are presently only 120 general practitioners (GPs) who are the certified assessors.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I want to declare that I am not one of them.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I am glad that under CareShield Life, there will be an increased pool of assessors to include occupational therapists, physiotherapists and nurses.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Assessors had given feedback that, presently, the grading levels for each ADL can be quite small and slight, making it hard to assess the patients.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Other feedback includes requests for assessment forms to be made more user-friendly.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Stroke patients are often struck with severe disability.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: While I can understand that women live longer, I feel that there can be better inclusiveness and fairness.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: My concern is that women may have lesser means to pay for premiums compared to men.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Women are earning less due to family commitments and may have even lesser savings to spare with increasing age.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I welcome the provision for people who are disabled at the age of 30 years to join and to receive payouts immediately after paying for one premium.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: This reflects the inclusive society that we aspire to build.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: But I am saddened that this idea of inclusive society does not extend to gender equity by requiring women to pay higher premiums for CareShield Life.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: I hope the Minister will reconsider on this one.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Many will not be able to afford the premiums.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: The other options of long-term care, apart from homecare and community care, are care in nursing homes, community hospitals, as well as day-care and palliative care centres.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: While we address the financial issue of long-term care with the implementation of CareShield Life, it is vital to continue providing the infrastructure for long-term care for the severely disabled who need institutional care.

speaker: Dr Lily Neo (Jalan Besar)
text: Of course, daycare centres and nursing homes will have to be increased in number and in quality, and I hope that MOH will also provide humane palliative care with better support and services.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, when it comes to preparing Singaporeans for their long-term care needs, the Motion under discussion today, CareShield Life, is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: There is a saying that we have children so that they can look after us when we grow old.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: But today in Singapore, depending solely on our children for care at old age is clearly not enough.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: As our population ages, the challenges of long-term elder care become ever greater.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Many people say we depend on ourselves, be it under disability insurance plans, such as CareShield Life or ElderShield, we all have to pay the premiums ourselves in order to receive payouts.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Yes, it is probably fair to say that, to a certain extent, we do depend on ourselves for our care.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: However, I think it would be more accurate to say that we depend on one another.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: We depend on one another to pool our risks together, so that we can pay relatively low, affordable premiums and receive relatively high, effective payouts.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: This is very much like the advertisements of insurance companies that say, "All for one, and one for all".

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Because I wish to remind everybody, especially the more elderly among us, that when we evaluate the premiums versus payouts and consider whether to convert from ElderShield to CareShield Life, we should remember this point: the more people we have pooling the risks, the more stable the premiums and payouts will be.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: CareShield Life is an enhanced version of Eldershield.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: What is more, CareShield Life will be administered by the Government, and not by the insurance companies.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The six ADLs are bathing, eating, changing clothes, going to the toilet, walking in the house, leaving the bed for the wheelchair or chair.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: From 2020, those who have reached 30 years of age with severe disabilities will be able to make claims under CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: They must first opt in and join CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Thereupon, when they are no longer able to look after themselves, whether because of stroke, ageing, dementia or otherwise, and cannot perform three out of the six ADLs, then they will be eligible to make a claim and receive monthly payouts in cash to help meet their mid- or long-term care needs for life, or until they fully recover.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Which direction should our social policies be aimed at?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: When our ideals are realised, people will not only look after their own family members or children, but the old will be cared for and the disabled looked after.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Through risk pooling, we pool our resources to look after the elderly and the disabled who cannot look after themselves.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The Committee says that CareShield Life should be self-sustainable, that is, a balance should be struck between the premiums received and payouts made and payouts should not outstrip premiums.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: But while the scheme may be self-sustainable, the details of its implementation, or even related work outside the ambit of the scheme, remain to be actively planned for and carried out.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: For example, how do we help and extend coverage to those who cannot afford the premiums, so that they will not be left behind?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Another example, $600 is more than $400 by $200.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: But how much more of long-term care can you buy with this additional amount?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: A full-time maid, nursing home or the day care centre – are there enough options of care available out there, even with $600 in your pockets?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: (In English): The Review Committee's recommendations are a step in the right direction for long-term care support.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: They embrace the principle of risk-pooling to address the growing needs of long-term care for those Singaporeans who, whether through age, illness or circumstance, become severely disabled.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: We welcome the Government’s commitment to providing that support to lower- and middle-income Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: For example, the initial cash payout of $600 per month under the enhanced scheme is higher than the $400 currently payable under ElderShield, but how much more long-term care it can help procure will depend on the mix of care alternatives available and how much they cost, such as home nursing, foreign domestic workers, a bed in a nursing home, a place in daycare centres and so on.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: For a real solution in providing long-term care to Singaporeans, quite beyond the payouts under a disability insurance scheme, such as CareShield Life, we need to develop an ecosystem rich in disability-care options, as well as effective policies that would nudge Singaporeans towards choices that meet not only individual demands for affordable and inclusive care, but also the public’s interests in sustainable care.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: An American politician said: "Without health insurance, getting sick or injured could mean going bankrupt, going without needed care or even dying needlessly".

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I think we can understand the context why the American politician said this.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This would benefit not just the aged in our population, but also the younger demographics who are increasingly aware of the importance of healthcare security for their future.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am also heartened by the efforts taken to ensure the scheme is inclusive by providing additional support to ensure affordability.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But unfortunately, my wife thinks it is selective inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That said, based on feedback and queries from my engagement with unionists and grassroots leaders, there are some clarifications that I would like to seek from the Minister with regard to CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In terms of policy administration, I would like to ask the Minister the rationale of having the MOH to administer the CareShield Life Scheme.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I understand from the White Paper that it simplifies administration and will be carried out on a not-for-profit basis.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is without a doubt that, by having the Government administer the policy, it would be easier to adjust the scheme as necessary.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, this then begs the question why was not the same considerations given when ElderShield was first introduced?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The decision to have MOH administer CareShield Life implies that there are inherent drawbacks or disadvantages if the scheme is to be administered by private insurance companies.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What are some of the key lessons that we have learnt from ElderShield that led to the decision for the new CareShield Life to be managed by MOH?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There is also this thinking that the private sector can be more efficient than the public sector in providing services or public goods.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: With MOH managing CareShield Life, would there be equal efficiency in the handling of insurance for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The report also shared that MOH will monitor the scheme closely and make the necessary adjustments to the scheme.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Would the policyholders be consulted before such changes, and is there the possibility of a lower payout being rendered in the future?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe that the CareShield Life scheme can provide a great opportunity to incentivise Singaporeans to lead a healthy and active lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given the worrying statistics on issues like diabetes and our efforts to promote healthy ageing, we should leverage the CareShield Scheme Premium subsidies to promote Singaporeans to lead an active lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is certainly better for a Singaporean not having to make a claim on his insurance and that starts with prevention by choosing a healthy lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Under the proposed CareShield Life, claims are allowed once the insured is unable to perform three out of six essential ADLs.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I do appreciate that setting a lower benchmark would mean higher premiums.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, can we consider a lower payout for Singaporeans affected with one or two disabilities?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given our ageing population, long-term care will continue to be a pressing concern for Singaporeans moving forward.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is our duty as the Government to not only ensure that we can provide the best level of healthcare to our citizens, but also to make sure that their financial situation would not take a drastic turn due to expensive healthcare.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I know this will incur a huge Government expenditure but, it can also give Singaporeans peace of mind for the added healthcare insurance.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   I give my full support towards the national long-term care insurance scheme called CareShield Life that provides financial aid to those afflicted with severe disability.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This scheme is better compared to ElderShield that is run by the private sector.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can the Government bear the costs to convert all ElderShield members to this new CareShield Life scheme?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is meant to encourage them to take more proactive steps to look after their physical health.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, in conclusion, given our ageing population, long-term care will continue to be a pressing concern for Singaporeans moving ahead.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is our duty as the Government to not only ensure that we can provide the best level of healthcare to our citizens, but also to make sure that their financial situation would not take a drastic turn due to expensive healthcare.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A few years ago, the Government announced MediShield Life which managed to give much assurance to many of us who are concerned with our ability to shoulder unexpected high hospitalisation costs.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: CareShield Life is another step in the right direction that would provide added peace of mind for many of us.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I personally welcome the CareShield Life Scheme as it will provide those afflicted by severe disabilities higher payouts for life, compared to ElderShield.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a good scheme which will benefit Singaporeans as the financial aid will provide an additional layer of social security.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: CareShield Life is particularly relevant for a rapidly ageing society like ours.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We will face, in the near future, every one out of four Singaporeans who is 65 and above, in view of the increasing number of these age-related disability cases to be expected.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that this scheme will be accepted by most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because the lifelong coverage and higher payouts are major improvements upon ElderShield’s benefits.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Therefore, the auto-conversion will provide convenience to ElderShield policyholders of all ages, compared to requiring them to sign up for CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The proposed participation incentives can be converted into subsidies for the various age groups.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I also hope that the Government will allow ElderShield supplement policyholders, who have already paid additional premiums for higher or longer monthly payouts, to port these premiums to their new CareShield policies.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Once on CareShield, interested Singaporeans may have the option to approach private insurers for additional coverage and payouts.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Instead, may I suggest allowing CareShield policyholders the option of higher payouts if they can afford the additional premiums?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If they should want to opt out of CareShield Life, they need to provide valid reasons, such as having similar disability insurance coverage with private insurers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, I would like to suggest that we recruit Singaporeans, as we did for PG, as Ambassadors to visit individuals and households who have opted out of ElderShield or CareShield to explain and assure them of the support by the Government, including financial assistance, to encourage them to join the new scheme.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The grassroots organisations (GROs) can work with the volunteers to identify and offer all necessary assistance to the households who need financial help and also encourage them to stay in the scheme.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   	CareShield Life is a good plan to provide more protection for Singaporeans with severe disabilities with lifetime cash payouts.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This helps to pay for long-term care and reduces the financial burden on patients and their families.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The scheme is generally supported by residents, but some have expressed confusion about the names of various Government programmes, in particular, CareShield Life and MediShield.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Chinese names of these two schemes are too similar, with only one character difference and, especially for the elderly, it is not easy to spot the difference.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In order for me to explain this new scheme easily, I have tried different ways.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many people do not want to listen, because they feel this topic is "inauspicious".

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I tried to use a simple name to explain this scheme – "Ping An 123" (Peace 123).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Why call it "Ping An 123"? "Three" symbolises coverage from age 30; "two" for the benefit of two parties, that is, the patient and their caregivers, hence, both the family members and the patient will benefit; "one" for lifetime payouts, every month you would receive payouts until recovery or death.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That is why I call it "Ping An 123".

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With this insurance, you will have peace of mind until death.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Anyway, I hope that Singaporeans can stay healthy, exercise more and prevent diseases.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Because if you fall ill, it is you yourself who will suffer.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every resident says to me that they do not want to burden their family members.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
