text: Precisely because we do not want to burden our family members that I encourage them to consider joining CareShield Life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I am concerned that the three aims make up an impossible trinity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is what economists would call a trilemma.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It means that, no matter how well and enlightened the design may be, it is impossible for CareShield Life to be inclusive, affordable and sustainable at the same time.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The first issue is that CareShield Life compromises inclusivity in two ways.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I find it objectionable that women are being penalised for something that is not within their control, being born women, when lifestyle choices within the control of individuals are not being treated as risk factors for premium calculation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: CareShield Life is to be a publicly administered compulsory insurance providing for universal social protection.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This means that, unlike privately run insurance schemes, risk-pooling should be done in such a way as to maximise the utility of social protection for all groups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why then are we splitting the population divisively into men and women?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why are men paying only for fellow men who become disabled, and women paying only for fellow women who become disabled?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have said this for CPF Life payouts and this bears repeating.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe Singaporean men, who are husbands, fathers and sons, would not begrudge risk-pooling to subsidise women who would have done so much unpaid care-work out of love as mothers, wives and daughters, and who would have far lesser savings than men in general.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why not extend auto-enrolment to ElderShield members aged 51-60 and above, which would cover all the ElderShield members?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this because the older ElderShield members have less MediSave savings to cover the base and catch-up premiums they have to pay to join CareShield Life?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But the Government is already committed to helping existing ElderShield members through subsidies and other interventions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, why not enrol the other cohort, too?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The second issue is that in trying to be affordable and inclusive, is CareShield Life compromising on sustainability?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I find it hard to square the argument that with the Government administering CareShield Life, we will get better economies of scale, when the same Government has been saying that farming out ElderShield competitively to three private insurers is a cost-effective system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do believe that a publicly administered social insurance scheme can do better than the three private insurers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But this begs the question: why was ElderShield farmed out to the three private insurers in the first place?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister does not seem to think the private insurers have profited handsomely in the answer to my February 2017 Parliamentary Question on ElderShield premiums and surpluses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But clearly, there is a difference, or else the Government would not be going for public administration of CareShield Life.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: So, what is the difference between the old ElderShield model and the new CareShield Life model, in terms of costs, profits and surpluses?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is not an academic question of public policy analysis or a question of history, as ElderShield will still be around.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This ties into my other question here about limiting auto-enrolment to ElderShield members aged 41-50.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would not allowing the older cohort to continue with ElderShield as administered by private insurers mean that their interests are being compromised, if public management is better?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If most existing ElderShield members make the switch to CareShield Life, would not this make a much reduced ElderShield membership pool unsustainable for a competitive system of three private insurers?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would this end up penalising the remaining ElderShield members?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why not nationalise ElderShield altogether and make the safety net truly universal, clear and clearer?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On what facts is this statistic based on?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Is this 50% statistic used in the actuarial model to derive the premiums?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One thing for sure, the health profile and, therefore, disability risk profile of younger cohorts, to be covered by CareShield Life, would not be the same as the older cohort today.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The younger cohorts should lead healthier life, given better nutritional, lifestyle, environmental and healthcare conditions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As such, is 50% chance not an extreme profiling of the population in terms of severe disability risk?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the end, it is a matter of balance and tradeoffs between the three aims and the Government has to explain this in greater detail and clarity to an educated public who wants to know the deal they are being compelled into.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While we support the Motion, the questions I am asking here are intended to achieve this, namely, greater clarity on the tradeoffs that the Government has decided on with CareShield Life.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I know there is this "gender rating" which is somewhat similar to car insurance where teenagers are made to pay a higher premium as they are seen as higher risks because of their age and lack of experience.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, in the case of CareShield Life, I think the argument that women have childbirth and they tend to live longer lives should not apply.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I feel, with the advancement in medicine, the risk during childbirth is very minimal.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: According to the Registry of Births and Deaths, maternal mortality or the death of a mother during childbirth, is relatively rare in Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It has even dropped to 2.3 per 1,000 births before.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: One can argue that men go for more dangerous sports and they are a higher risk.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I would want to believe that women are just as careful with their health, if not more careful than men.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why is there no increase after the claim is made?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Surely, after the claim is made, inflation and the rising of medical costs still goes on.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Presumably, this is because the inclusion of people with pre-existing conditions will increase the number of claims and thus increase the premiums everyone else needs to pay.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But can this not be addressed by excluding the claims related to their pre-existing conditions, while allowing them to claim for other conditions?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, in 2003, when I went for a major operation for colon cancer, the insurance company did not want to insure me.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But five years later, they said I can be insured, but anything related to cancer, not covered.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe this would need another exercise to warn the elderly to take precautions at an age when they are most vulnerable so that they can avoid disability where possible.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   The launch of CareShield Life has put many Singaporeans’ minds at ease.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First, after a person has made a claim from CareShield Life, the amount of payouts will cease to increase.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, he continues to face inflation and the rise of medical costs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Why then can the payout not also increase in tandem?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Second, for those with pre-existing conditions, they cannot convert from ElderShield to CareShield Life.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that the inclusion of people with pre-existing conditions will increase the number of claims, thus increase the premiums that everyone else needs to pay.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, can we consider excluding claims relating to their pre-existing conditions while, at the same time, allowing them to still join CareShield Life?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Third, and also the most important point: why are the premiums for women higher?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In Nee Soon South, very early in the morning, we see many women going to National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) FairPrice, Sheng Shiong and the market to buy daily necessities that their family would need.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They carry many bags of fish, meat, vegetables and fruits and bring them home.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: After that, they will hurriedly go to work.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Housewives would be busy with housework all day long.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: During the weekends, many of those who join community club activities are also women, taking part in Zumba, line dancing and so on.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, the fact that women live longer should not be a surprise to us.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure that men here in this Parliament would also agree with me that women should pay the same premiums as men.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: At the launch of the scheme in 2002, more than a third of eligible Singaporeans and Permanent Residents aged 40 to 69 opted out of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: For some reason, the share of eligible residents not covered by ElderShield remained roughly the same, 15 years later, in 2017.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I did not find the benefits of ElderShield meaningful and assuring back in 2002.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Even after the scheme was reviewed in 2007, my opinion of the scheme remained unchanged.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The current review, however, is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Similar to the review done in 2007, the definition of "severe disability" was left untouched again in the review of 2018.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As Ms Sylvia Lim has pointed out earlier, I also find the criteria to file a claim under ElderShield too strict to begin with.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: A 2018 review report on ElderShield has a passing mention of some focus group participants suggesting some payouts upon mild or moderate disability instead of upon severe disability, but that suggestion was glossed over with a statement that the Review Committee preferred to prioritise, and I quote, "critical benefit enhancements to payout duration and quantum" in order to keep the enhanced scheme affordable.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If anyone of you is unable to eat on your own and use the toilet on your own, you are not deemed severely disabled.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If you are unable to move from room to room or move from a bed to an upright chair on your own, you are also not counted as severely disabled under ElderShield.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Why was this part of ElderShield not put under any review?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It is stated in the review report that many of the projections and parameters for formulating the enhanced scheme are based on local data and supplemented by international data.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Did the Committee review any international data on the approach to define severe disability versus ElderShield’s definition, which has remained unchanged since 2002?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: If Japan, which has the highest percentage of senior citizens in the world, is deemed the most lenient in claims criteria for long-term care insurance across countries compared in the review report, would that make Singapore the least lenient then, looking at the comparison?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The 2018 review of ElderShield calls for expanding the insurance coverage to achieve greater inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Would it not be reasonable to expect the enhanced scheme to have a more inclusive definition of severe disability as well?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Surely, inclusivity must also mean helping more people stricken with disability, beyond achieving universal coverage for all.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Next, it was stated in the review report that premiums for the proposed CareShield Life should be adjusted regularly to take into account changes in payout quantum and claims experience.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: It also lists investment returns on the insurance fund as one of the factors affecting the pricing of premiums.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: CareShield Life is supposed to be self-funding based on actuarial calculations and risk-pooling approach.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The insurance fund accumulated should not be invested in high-risk instruments to begin with.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The report also acknowledged that the role of insurance should be strengthened to play a more prominent part to help Singaporeans prepare for their long-term care needs, while Government subsidies, personal savings and family support will continue to be the main source of support in this area.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: At this point, I welcome what the Minister said earlier in allowing members to withdraw cash from their MediSave accounts to support their long-term care needs.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I have one clarification to seek on this point.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Can someone who is deemed not so severely disabled by CareShield Life apply for such withdrawal, that is, that person can only perform two instead of three ADLs?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: CareShield Life is superior to ElderShield in many ways.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Universal insurance coverage is also a good thing but it should not be oversold with projections and assumptions that are bordering on paranoia.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I wish to ask the Minister how the premiums for CareShield Life are determined.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Is it based on a doomsday scenario that one in two healthy Singaporeans aged 65 today could become severely disabled in their lifetime or based on actual claim experience from ElderShield?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: As rightly stated in the review report, "it is challenging to accurately project claims experience, longevity and disability trends decades in advance." So, there is no need to stress and repeat that half our population could become severely disabled in time to come just to bring CareShield Life into existence.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I note the Minister's explanation on this rather depressing statement.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Based on what the Minister has said, all of us would be severely disabled in our lifetime anyway, when we are nearer our deathbed.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I believe CareShield Life can stand on its own merit.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also wish to add to the messages of congratulations to the ESRC for rendering a very thoughtful report.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note from the speeches made by Members before me that these recommendations have broad support from both sides of the House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is welcome because medical improvements have increased and will continue to increase the lifespan of our disabled residents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Building in a mechanism to increase the payouts over time will allow the payouts to keep up with inflationary pressures.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some hon Members have suggested that the $600 per month may not be enough.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my view, we need to look at all the other schemes that come into play, for example, the concessionary Foreign Domestic Worker (FDW) levy of $60 per month, so that the full picture of support that the Government gives can be appreciated.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The consequence of the enhancements has resulted in the adoption of the universal coverage so that there is risk-pooling and the premiums are kept affordable.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support this approach, subject to the case made by the hon Member and Chairman of the GPC for Health, Dr Chia Shi-Lu, on equalising premiums payable by males and females.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This point was echoed by several other Members.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The set up of the ElderFund and the provision of premium subsidies are a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am, therefore, concerned about the impact of easing this requirement on the premiums.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If not, how much more subsidies are expected from the Government, and what would be the financial impact of providing more subsidies than what is currently contemplated?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A clarification on these issues will be welcomed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have three questions: first, what is the average life expectancy of disabled residents who are able to make a claim under the current ElderShield and how is this expected life expectancy of such residents expected to increase in the coming decades?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, how does the assessment of disability by reference to ADLs apply to mentally disabled Singapore residents?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As may be recalled by Members of this House, I asked MOH and MSF in this House to reconsider the application of the ADL criterion with respect to the provision of concessionary FDW levy for mentally and intellectually disabled residents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: MSF and MOH announced earlier this year that for such residents, they have introduced the Client Assessment Form (CAF) to assess such residents' cognitive disability.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Can a similar approach be taken vis-a-vis CareShield Life, please?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Ultimately, the mentally disabled and physically disabled residents are in the same boat as they are unemployable, need to be taken of by their caregivers and, therefore, would benefit from CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some mental conditions can be linked to physical conditions, for example, dementia.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But some are not, for example, Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am aware of several families in Bukit Batok who have severely autistic children and are concerned about their long-term care needs, and they may benefit from the more flexible approach.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, I recognise that there is a need to deter the making of false claims because such claims would, in effect, raise premiums.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, what safeguards would be put in place to make sure that no false claims are filed and processed?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My last point, Mr Speaker, Sir, what is the status of Singapore residents who subsequently lose their Singapore citizenship or residency?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this regard, I note that the system, as promulgated, is only made workable as a result of Government resources and money being spent to run the insurance system and provide premium subsidies in additional support to Singapore residents.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What would be the position of Singapore residents who lose their residency or Singapore citizenship status?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I see two scenarios because the coverage under CareShield Life and cash payouts are for their entire lives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One scenario is where Singapore residents who make payment of the premiums until they reach the age of 67 and they do not need to make premium payouts anymore and, subsequently, they give up their Singapore citizenship.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Would they still be allowed payments under this scheme?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Another scenario, which I think is less likely, is where Singapore residents receive CareShield payouts and then lose their residency or citizenship.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A clarification on these points would be most welcome.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Any one of us may be stricken with disability in old age.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are many of us who have been.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We should not leave Singaporeans to bear the ravages of genetic roulette on their own.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Risk-pooling is a sensible way to address the increasing incidence of chronic disease and disability that come with an ageing population.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Risk-pooling stands alongside the other policy prong that is needed here, of course, which is prevention in the form of encouragement to living more healthily, health screening and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On the whole, the merits of long-term care insurance far outweigh the downsides.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I agree with the other points made by Workers’ Party Members, in particular, the point about gender equality made by Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Pritam Singh and Assoc Prof Daniel Goh.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will focus my speech on a few themes – affordability, transparency, efficiency and creating more options for the payouts to be spent for maximum effect.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are premiums set at the right level such that the capital adequacy and medical loss ratio for the scheme is aligned with similar government schemes elsewhere in the developed world?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: No doubt none of us has a crystal ball.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But have premium levels been set such that we are not likely to accumulate unexpectedly high levels of reserves relative to payouts in future?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This would appear to be a pessimistic assumption given that, for example, in the United States (US), the comparable figure, based on one source, is 35.4%, based on a definition of disability that would appear to be far wider than the criteria specified for payouts under CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Tied to this is another point: have premium rebates been factored into the calculations for premiums and payouts?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some long-term care schemes do actually build future premium rebates into the actuarial model that determines premiums and this practice is not necessarily wrong.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, how do we guard against the possibility that the calculations have over-reserved for future premium rebates and, hence, have set premiums too high for the current generation?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Also, on affordability, the report states that those who cannot afford to pay premiums even after means-tested subsidies will be given additional help.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some individuals may have a per capita household income that disqualifies them from many financial assistance schemes but may also have a very high expenditure profile for reasons out of their control, such as their medical situation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How will such cases be evaluated for additional help?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This leads me to my second broad point, which is transparency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What assumptions were made about how many residents will become disabled?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What was the basis for these assumptions – data on chronic disease incidence coupled with data on demographic projections?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Milliman Limited and Deloitte Actuaries and Consultants, respected global professional firms, contributed to the report, the latter being the appointed actuary of the MediShield scheme.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I do not expect the actuarial model used to be suspect.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the assumptions and policy decisions behind any model can and should be subjected to reasonable public scrutiny and debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Related to this is the question of what if payouts fall below assumptions?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Premium rebates are considered once every five years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From the report, it would appear that awarding such rebates will be up to the independent Council and there is no mandatory rule on awarding premium rebates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How do we ensure that the independent Council does not over-reserve funds from the current generation’s premiums for future generations, and makes the right determination on what is fair intergenerationally?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can transparent rules be adopted to guide them?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There could be efficiencies in having the Government operate the scheme, as the profit motive is absent and there are greater potential economies of scale from administering the entire pot of funds centrally.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, there are also risks since the returns on existing reserves and the cost of administration are not subjected to competitive market discipline.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How will the Government ensure that the funds are managed efficiently and that administrative costs will be minimal?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Will there be rigorous benchmarking of administrative costs of private insurers and those of other benchmark-worthy government schemes in developed countries?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What strategies will be used to invest the funds accumulated in the reserves to earn a reasonable return while adopting low risk?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The ElderShield report mentions that CPF Board should be engaged for administration of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This debate should not only be about the quantum of premiums and payouts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It should also be about how we create an ecosystem rich with options for those who receive payouts to spend them with optimum effectiveness for themselves and society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Right now, the elderly disabled have various options for managing their condition.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They can subsist based only on family care or self-care at home.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Or they can enrol in an integrated home and day care package.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But IHDC is as yet not widely prevalent.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Home care, day care and IHDC have the potential to yield strong benefits in terms of: firstly, enabling the elderly to still live with their family in many cases, which is immensely meaningful; secondly, allowing family members who play some caregiving role to work during the day, thus enhancing our labour force participation rate; thirdly, limiting the growth in the foreign worker population, if local full-time and part-time employees and volunteers are optimally engaged; and fourthly, enabling the elderly disabled to remain within the communities to which they have grown attached.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Hong Kong, most people have an elder day care centre within a few kilometres of their home.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This contributes to a good universal long-term care network as it enables optimum caregiving in situ, as being close to home, and familiar neighbourhood social support networks can help to make for quality eldercare.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In Singapore, one huge advantage we have on this front is the presence of Housing and Development Board (HDB) void decks, which can be used for day care centres that do not incur exorbitant private rental costs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In particular, for day care, take-up may depend on the proximity of day care centres to homes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Are the number and availability of day care places trending in the right direction to make this a viable option in future?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Doing so would make CareShield a meaningful part of this nation’s response to ageing and to the imperative to create a fairer and thus better society for all Singaporeans to call home.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.50 pm until 4.15 pm.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First of all, I would like to record my sincere appreciation to ESRC for the immense hard work.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The elderly and vulnerable are groups of Singaporeans whom I hold close to my heart.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And CareShield Life is, in my opinion, a scheme that is crucial for their well-being.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As Singaporeans live longer lives, this also means the increased probability of having a severe disability that requires long-term care.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And with more Singaporeans having few or no children, it would also be unrealistic to completely rely on the younger generation to pick up the tab.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When I go on my walkabouts and during my Meet-the-People sessions, it is a common sight to see wheelchair-bound residents going about with a caregiver, often, an FDW, in tow.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These senior citizens are the more fortunate ones.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The less well-off are home-bound, constantly being cooped up, which hampers one's well-being.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To continue having a quality of life even with severe disability, it is important to have adequate funds to tap on in old age.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am pleased to note that the Committee has made a change to the nomenclature for ElderShield, which I had advocated many times previously.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The new name CareShield more accurately reflects the core of the scheme, which is to become a key pillar of Singapore's social safety net, giving care to all Singaporeans regardless of their age and background.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some young people are indignant about having to start as early as 30 years old.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There has even been talk that this is a ploy to get the young to pay for the old.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For one, severe disabilities can happen to anyone at any age.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a factor that is lacking in many private insurance schemes, and this is why there is a need for CareShield Life to shore up and fill up the gaps.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is good practice to start taking ownership of one's health from a young age.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And to reward those who do so, I wish to recommend offering incentives on top of what will be given, such as a discount on premiums for the following year, for those under ElderShield 300 and ElderShield 400, who had not made prior claims.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This will encourage them to opt into it.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It also reinforces the notion of taking responsibility for good health.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In cases where patients recover from their disabilities, there must be proper communication and follow-up with them on their health and financial status to ensure a smooth transition.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This process must be handled with sensitivity and with compassion, as the claimants adjust from the position of receiving monthly CareShield payouts, to the state of the termination of payouts.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Furthermore, in order to remain covered under CareShield for the future, these recovered policyholders have to resume premium payments.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The healthcare institution where he receives rehabilitation would have the relevant records, and their cooperation is essential so that CPF Board receives the necessary updates without inconveniencing the policyholder.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I note that a Panel is consulted with regard to adjustment of premiums.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Understandably, actuaries who work with the insurance profession will be consulted for their expertise.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I would request that social workers, healthcare workers, VWOs and people who work with the disadvantaged be invited to join the Panel to share their observations and opinions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Healthcare professionals could offer precious input on health matters, such as the average remaining lifespan and needs of a severely disabled person.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government is also offering participation incentives spread over 10 years to entice existing cohorts to opt into CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Despite these incentives, the calculations are complex at a glance and, if money is a concern, some people may think it is simply more cost-saving to stay on ElderShield or for those who had opted out of Eldershield, not to sign up at all.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As mentioned earlier, I hope the Government will consider my recommendation of offering additional incentives to ElderShield 300 and ElderShield 400 policyholders to get onboard CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Meanwhile, older Singaporeans are expected to pay a base premium and a catch-up component on top of their yearly premiums.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While this is reasonable, I fear that they will be turned off by the idea of having to pay more at an age when job stability is a concern, and this is the very group that is most vulnerable and susceptible to disabilities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to start a comprehensive public education campaign to convince Singaporeans about the necessity of CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Imagine how confused the older, less educated people, who would stand to benefit most from such policies, would be.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government must provide resources for people to turn to for advice and guidance.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Preferably, these education campaigns should involve counsellors who can offer advice on the importance and responsibility of preparing for retirement.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There should be qualified professionals who can provide a free one-on-one consultation session to explain and compare the various Government insurance policies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): With regard to platforms for the education campaign, we have to bear in mind that people these days have little time for the newspapers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: They prefer to rely on social media, and simply just skim through the headlines.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government must reach out to all age groups, both young and old, using appropriate platforms without trivialising the subject matter.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would CareShield be adequate to address potential needs?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For those who can afford to pay for an enhanced component, this would also spur insurance providers to improve their plans and provide better coverage.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government could moderate integrated policy premiums so that they remain reasonably priced.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Nevertheless, it is human nature to be sceptical of matters that one does not fully understand.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I urge the Government to step up on outreach programmes to help as many Singaporeans as possible to benefit from this scheme.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This provides better protection to those suffering from disabilities, as I am sure that with a better living environment and better medical care, there will be more who will outlive the six-year limit on payouts under the current ElderShield.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But while CareShield Life is an improvement, I do have some concerns that I would like to raise.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, let me touch on the qualification for payouts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In many cases, being unable to perform two ADLs, or even one ADL, such as the inability to transfer yourself from your bed to a wheelchair, would be considered a severe impairment to living life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Because in some instances, help may come too late if we wait until one loses his ability to perform three ADLs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, I would like to ask the Minister if MOH knows how many Singaporeans who have at least three ADLs today and are currently under ElderShield coverage have made claims or are receiving payouts?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My point is how can we help to ensure that those who are severely disabled, who are the most in need of the payouts, would have an easy time qualifying for them?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would they have to travel to the hospital to be assessed, or could local GPs do house calls to make the assessment?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How many GPs are there currently qualified to make such house calls, and how can we simplify the assessment process so that those in need would not have to wait for an inordinate amount of time before receiving their payouts?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many residents whom I spoke to question if $600 would be a sufficient amount, taking into consideration the challenges faced by one who is severely disabled, one who has inability to perform three ADLs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is not difficult to imagine that those defined as such would require the constant help of a caregiver.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But $600 would be insufficient to pay for the employment of one domestic helper.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Next, I would like to touch on the transitional subsidies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is the rationale for providing the subsidy only for the first five years after the introduction of CareShield Life?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What about those who will be 30 years old from 2025?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Should they not also be eligible for such transitional subsidy?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: According to the 2017 Labour Force Report by the Ministry of Manpower, women are more likely than men to stay outside the labour force, and they made up 64% of residents outside the labour force in 2017.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Family responsibilities were the top reason given which kept females outside the labour force.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: According to a study by a consumer research firm, Value Penguin, also released last year in 2017, men earn nearly 20% more than women in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And in some industries, this wage gap can be as much as 40%.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am not a woman but, surely, we can find means to collectively offset the projected increase in healthcare spending for women due to their longer lifespan.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many Members have already spoken to ask for equality in premiums and I hope MOH can seriously consider having equal payment of premiums for both men and women.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While it is reassuring that the Government has guaranteed that no Singaporean will lose coverage due to the inability to pay their premiums, many are concerned if premiums will remain affordable in future.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A recent news article reported that insurers offering IPs have made losses for the second year in a row.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And with that, news reports say there is a possible increase in IP premiums in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would premiums for CareShield Life eventually become an expensive burden for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Before I conclude, I would like to provide feedback on the public communications on CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I have asked many residents what they thought of the proposed scheme.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A common response is that the scheme is simply too complicated.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Individuals do not quite understand how the scheme would impact them personally.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How much premiums would I need to pay?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would my premiums continue to increase over time?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What happens if I lose my job and cannot afford to pay the premiums for the period when I am unemployed?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: After each session, I find myself learning new information about the scheme.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I am certain that our MOH officers are working very hard to communicate the scheme to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But the challenge remains that the scheme impacts individuals differently.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Perhaps the Ministry can consider setting up a CareShield Life hotline or, in today's technology, a chatbot, to address individual's concerns and queries more comprehensively.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I support the introduction of CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It will impact many people for many years, both in terms of care as well as costs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many countries the world over are grappling with increased healthcare costs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Australia, the Productivity Commission considered healthcare spending to be Australia's greatest future fiscal challenge, with its share in gross domestic product rising from 6.5% to 10.8% in 2060.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Canada, a study by a non-partisan research institute projected a budget deficit, due to increased healthcare spending and income transfer to seniors by 2045.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: More urgently, a study by Japan researchers show that Asian countries are ageing more quickly than European countries, giving them less time to react or plan for social spending.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, Japan faces a 2025 problem when Japan's baby boomers hit 75 and older – the age at which government subsidies increase drastically.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Already taking up one-third of the budget, healthcare spending in 2025 is projected to increase by about 30% from the spend in 2015, with a budget deficit problem commencing between 2021 and 2024.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even though our social support system here in Singapore is structured differently from these countries, funding healthcare remains a pressing issue, and lessons from overseas remain relevant to us.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While private insurance that insure against disabilities focus on making up for the inability to work, long-term care is often overlooked or neglected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This may be because the possibility of being disabled does not cross a person's mind.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Sometimes, it may be that there are other more pressing, urgent financial needs – the children's education, the parent's medical bills – these are legitimate needs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But when it comes to a national policy of budgeting for the nation, we cannot just focus on our current needs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And this is where I see CareShield Life coming in.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: CareShield Life offers lifetime payouts in the event of a severe disability until recovery.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: ElderShield would give payouts up to six years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even though this may be enough for more than half of the people who become severely disabled, three in 10 need long-term care for more than 10 years.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lifetime payouts make sure caregivers and individuals do not need to worry about what would happen if this source of help dries up before recovery.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Pritam Singh raised the issue of affordability of premiums.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chen Shao Mao did too, and Ms Sylvia Lim alluded to the fact that the Workers' Party will be addressing this point.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Do we want to ensure affordability of premiums?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But how do we translate those wishes into reality?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Let us look at the hard facts to see what the Government will do to make the premiums more affordable for fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, the premiums are designed such that the annual MediSave contributions for most working households is sufficient to cover the premium entirely.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For those with a monthly per capita household income of $1,100 or less, it is a 30% subsidy rate.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This helps to balance premium affordability with the scheme's sustainability.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Those twinned priorities of affordability and sustainability are of equal significance, equal importance, for our current Singaporeans and future Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Switzerland, although the long-term care insurance is sustainable, affordability is a concern.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2015, the average annual premiums were around $5,000.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, unlike Japan, where premiums start at 40 years old and continue to be payable until death, premiums for CareShield Life are only payable during the working years of a person's life, from 30 years old to the re-employment age of 67 years old.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here is another statistic to show what the Government is doing to balance affordability with sustainability.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The premium payout for those who become severely disabled for 10 years from age 67 to 76, the payouts received are about 12 times the premiums paid.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And if the person was eligible for subsidies, payouts are about 18 times the premiums paid.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yes, we want to ensure that premiums remain affordable even in the future.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the slew of measures I have touched on so far provides a formidable and financially sound precedent for the people who will be reviewing premiums in future to consider.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Essentially, I hope the message is that what the Government is stating today is to take care to ensure that there are measures in place to ensure premium reviews are done with caution and with a slew of measures to assist Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And this is the way we do things in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, the White Paper recommends additional premium support by the Government beyond subsidies as the last resort to ensure that no one will drop out of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, because it is prefunded, we need not worry that our children's generation is shouldering the load of the scheme.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The effect of a smaller population will be minimised and the scheme will be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While this is different from other countries, such as Japan, South Korea, Germany and Switzerland, where they use a pay-as-you-go system, this system is one that is more sustainable and equitable for long-term care where the costs increase with the age of the cohort.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, the CD Howe Institute suggested that the Canadian province of New Brunswick mitigates the impact of rising costs in some healthcare services by selectively converting some particularly age-sensitive costs to prefunding instead of pay-as-you-go, example, long-term care.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some countries with pay-as-you-go schemes are struggling with the financial sustainability of the schemes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, Japan is exploring raising co-payment from 10% or tightening the eligibility criteria.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: South Korea is looking into raising the percentage of the income being contributed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, Mr Speaker, I would submit, the way we have structured it in Singapore as a pre-funded universal scheme helps to balance both present affordability as well as future sustainability.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And to remain responsible stewards for future generations, I would say that we need to balance the equal priorities of affordability and financial sustainability.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me to move on to a different topic of my speech, Sir, on payouts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In terms of payouts, CareShield Life comes in the form of cash and not in the form of service.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is good, because it gives the individual and caregiver more flexibility in arranging care.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It also accommodates the wide buffet of options out there.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But whether or not the payouts meaningfully relieve a burden for the long-term also depends on this question: are long-term care costs affordable?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In light of this, what has the Government done, or what will it do, to make sure that long-term care costs are kept affordable?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another feature of this scheme is that, over the years, as a person pays more premiums, the payout in the event of a severe disability also increases.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But if we think about it, when someone becomes severely disabled and receives a cash payout from CareShield Life, his or her future is still uncertain.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He or she does not know for how long she will need it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Yes, it is good that the payouts can continue to a lifetime, but how do we ensure they remain sufficient in light of inflation?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Medical inflation, I think, is higher than general inflation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another question I have is whether the severely disabled from the existing cohorts from CareShield Life will be excluded.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If they never had a chance to purchase ElderShield, arguably, more than anyone right now, they need the support which CareShield Life is going to provide to the future cohorts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another question I have is: if a person recovers from his or her severe disability and no longer receives payouts, what happens to his or her premium after that and at what level would the payouts be if the person fulfils the criteria at another time?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since CareShield Life has lifetime coverage and is universal, including those in future cohorts with pre-existing disabilities, if a person recovers, it makes sense, in my view, for him or her to still be enrolled under this scheme.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is important to keep this mandatory CareShield Life scheme sustainable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At page 29 of the well-written Report, it says, “Several large insurance companies have exited the long-term care insurance market due to unsustainable losses, while those that remained have sharply increased premiums and tightened their underwriting criteria.” That is for several large insurance companies.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, ensuring fiscal prudence for this endeavour is key.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Much work has been put in by the team at MOH, the Committee itself, and MOH working with many agencies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I would also like to record my thanks to the ESRC for the extensive work that has been done, as well as to the MOH team.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Planning for the time when one becomes severely disabled and thinking about long-term care requirements are not something that each of us necessarily thinks about.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We tend to think that disability would not happen to us.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is the general feedback that I get, especially from the young in the community.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And, for many, if we do become disabled, many have expressed that they do not want to prolong that state.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Unfortunately, in both of these circumstances, none of us can control these outcomes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Therefore, it is important that long-term care is something we plan for, because when one is disabled, there is a need for ongoing care and support, and caregivers as well as families are impacted.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And I would like to just share some examples that I have encountered in the community in my ward.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I have a resident who has seen me over the last few years.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: His challenge has been in providing long-term care for his mother.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: His mother is in a nursing home because she is disabled and the family has challenges taking care of her.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And where he is struggling is in paying for the nursing home charges.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, if there was long-term care planning done previously for her and, if she was of a cohort that had done long-term planning, that funding, that benefit payout, would have, in his case, helped a lot.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This lady, in her middle age, quite a few years ago, her husband had a sudden disability and he had to be bedridden.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: She continued working, looked at all the different helping hands support and, up to today, she is in a very difficult situation.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In fact, I saw her a couple of weeks ago, and she is still struggling to bring up the children as well as support the husband and give the care that the husband needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: You can see that it is not about just providing long-term care, but it is also the fact that because when someone is disabled, it affects the family as well.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Why I am sharing these examples is because while we talk about inclusion – and the recommendations have been on inclusion – there has also been a lot of discussion on the ground about exclusion.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And I think there needs to be a lot more in terms of helping people understand the need, even though the scheme is compulsory.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And as we have an ageing population, smaller families and people living longer, long-term care becomes even more important.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, while I understand that the priority – both for ElderShield and now CareShield – is to provide protection in old age.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The latter example that I shared shows that, regardless of one's age, economic and financial situation, the demands on long-term care do have an impact on both the individual and the caregivers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I would like now to touch on two areas – universal coverage and premium affordability and sustainability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This ensures that the coverage is inclusive, with everyone having basic financial protection for their long-term care cost.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As the Committee had noted, this will strengthen our social compact and is aligned with our values of an inclusive and, more importantly, a caring society which we strive to build.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Both the men and the women before me have said a lot on this point, but the point that I would like to make is that given the risk-pooling and the fact that we are making the scheme compulsory, it is only right that premiums should be equal, regardless of gender, and I hope that MOH will take this point into consideration.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While many can agree on the benefits of universal coverage and risk-pooling and participation for everyone from age 30 onwards, many in this age group are also at stages of their lives when they have multiple responsibilities.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For some of them, they are starting families, at the same time supporting ageing parents.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Hence, CareShield Life may be seen as an additional commitment on them financially.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For some in this cohort, they may already have coverage and this will be seen as a duplication and additional cost.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can the Minister share what consideration is being given to this and what does it mean for those who already have coverage which they have with private insurers?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Payouts are in cash and there is also no restriction on usage.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This flexibility is welcomed, as long-term care needs will differ from person to person, and long-term care itself will evolve.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we all know, whether it is informal care, home care services, nursing care, centre-based care as well as palliative care services, long-term care needs are quite strenuous financially, and this flexibility is definitely welcomed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With CareShield Life's enhanced payouts and benefits, there is still the question of premium affordability.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The recommendation to keep premiums low – besides risk-pooling that I touched on earlier as well as starting younger for the premiums to be spread across a longer period and also allowing for MediSave to be used to pay for premiums – does help in ensuring affordability because it eases the out-of-pocket expenses.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Despite this, there is a lot of questions around how the premium amounts have been arrived at.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can the Minister share more details about how premiums will be kept affordable over time?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: CareShield Life premium is another premium – apart from MediShield Life premium – that MediSave can be used for.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, MediSave is also used for other outpatient and inpatient needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, the question for many is "Will there be sufficient funds in MediSave for the premiums?" And with the changing models of employment – with freelance and contract work as well as the gig economy – incomes may not be as stable and, therefore, MediSave contributions may also be impacted.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But as long as AV is used, he or she would be automatically disqualified from the subsidies if this is the same case of how AV is going to be used for the means assessment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This being the case, this would also mean that per capita household incomes may not be considered because they have already not met the AV criterion.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, I hope that the Minister would consider how the AV criterion will be used for means-testing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The scheme itself is also, as many have mentioned today, fairly complex.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Before I start, I would like to thank the Committee which have presented a very good Report.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   	Before I start, I would like to express my thanks to the ESRC for producing an excellent report.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I join my fellow Members of Parliament in supporting the Motion tabled by the Health Minister just now.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He gave a comprehensive speech on the various schemes that are in place to provide support to our Citizens and Permanent Residents for their healthcare needs in the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, there are some issues I would like to seek clarification from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Currently, we have a number of insurance schemes, ranging from MediSave, MediShield, Integrated Shield, ElderShield300, ElderShield400, and now ElderFund and CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think many people are still grappling with the terms and conditions with regard to how to use these schemes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And, come 2020, they have to make informed decisions whether they want to opt for CareShield, and why they have to top up the premiums.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Unless one is working in the frontlines of the insurance industry, and unless one is also working in the frontlines of the healthcare industry handling claims and counselling patients on how to use the different schemes, many of them may not understand the impact of this enhancement to ElderShield.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope, at some point in the future, the Government would be able to streamline everything, simplify them and make them more digestible to the man-in-the-street.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I see it, it will be a mammoth exercise for the Government to explain this latest scheme to the masses.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many will, I foresee, perhaps merely catch a glimpse of what is being rolled out in the media.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is no doubt that the payment is made via MediSave, but this same MediSave is also used for the payment of MediShield Life and hospital expenses incurred over time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As our people get older and reach an advanced age, would there be sufficient funds in their MediSave to pay their premiums?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As it is, I believe there are cases where people can actually use up all their MediSave money for their treatment and, in such situations, how are they to pay the premiums for CareShield?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is especially true amongst the elderly who are no longer working.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, there is another group comprising self-employed workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some may not be able to afford to pay the premiums, especially the younger workers who may take up an odd job here and there, such as performing ad hoc delivery services, among others.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And to complicate matters further for this group, if they are staying with their parents, the AV of their home may not meet the threshold of $13,000 and below to be eligible for additional financial support.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During my constituency home visits, I do see seniors who stay in homes that are worth more than the AV of $13,000 but have no fixed income.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps they have just lost their life partner.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another question that I would like to ask the Minister is the different premiums for women.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am of the opinion that we should not differentiate the premium rates that women should pay.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Although statistically they are living longer, I think that all the men in this Chamber as well as the rest of Singapore will not object to providing this additional help for women, as they may be our own mothers, wives and daughters.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, it is important that this matter is resolved.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Another point I would like to ask is the withdrawal of funds for disabled persons under ElderFund.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I applaud the Minister for setting up this new fund to help lower-income Singaporeans who are severely disabled.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But what is the source of these funds for ElderFund?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we look at today’s prices, $50-$200 cannot buy us many things.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In 2020, the purchasing power could be less, taking into consideration inflation and other factors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, can the Minister consider reviewing this withdrawal limit when we are closer to the policy’s implementation?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, how do we safeguard those who are severely disabled to ensure that the withdrawal amount is sufficient, especially if they are also suffering from dementia or any other mental disabilities?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The need to have responsible family members or caregivers is a very important one, so that the money is spent wisely on the intended recipient and does not go into someone else’s pocket.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In people’s minds, they will say, "I am on ElderShield, and so what should I do?" For this group, they will be glad to know that they can upgrade to CareShield Life from 2021.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But if you do, you are required to pay more in terms of premiums.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, for those who have opted out from ElderShield, they can opt in to CareShield Life if they are not disabled.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, when this group reaches the crossroads where they are not on ElderShield, but yet have the option to choose CareShield Life coverage, how can the Government help these people to make informed decisions?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will reminders be sent to them to let them know that such options are available to them?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps it is good that the younger generation are given the choice whether or not they want to opt in or opt out.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As we all know, MediShield is compulsory as it covers hospitalisation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But younger people may have bought their own policies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, given that, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   MOH's CareShield Life is a very thoughtful initiative.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the past, Singaporeans were afraid of getting sick and not being able to afford the medical cost.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Today, if Singaporeans become bedridden, they will have CareShield Life as a protection so that they would not have any regret.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: A good policy needs to be communicated clearly to garner support from the people.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Therefore, I have three "big" questions and two small ones to ask the Minister.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: These questions should be explained patiently but acted upon quickly.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: At this age, people are still quite robust; their career would have just started, and they are beginning to have a family.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is a time when their living expenses are shooting up.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Few people would envisage that they could be severely disabled at some point.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So, I would like to ask the Minister, at this point in time, how many Singaporeans below the age of 40 are severely disabled?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In other words, out of $100 premiums that Singaporeans pay, the Government only need to pay out $4 to those severely disabled.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Logically, the payout rate of CareShield Life should be much lower.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Therefore, why do we ask people to start paying premiums from 30 years old?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If a Singaporean in his 30s and 40s is, indeed, severely disabled, then he will get a payout every month for several decades.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In fact, it is quite common for a 30-year-old to buy insurance.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many Singaporeans start to buy life insurance once they start to work.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The logic behind it is to prepare for rainy days when you are doing well.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, many Singaporeans are still not convinced that they must immediately join CareShield Life when they reach 30.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: So, I hope MOH can explain it in a way that they can easily understand, using illustrations if need be.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Therefore, in the next 10 years, the payout rate will be as low, or even lower, than that of ElderShield.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Minister also said that CPF Board will help invest the large sum of CareShield Life premiums, and the returns will also benefit insured Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Currently, the lowest interest rate of MediSave is 4%.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope that CPF can peg the returns on CareShield Life to the lowest MediSave interest rate so that even if CareShield Life payouts increase by 2% annually, the premiums need not be increased.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Third, since CareShield Life is described as a silver bullet by MOH, then we should intensify public education efforts so that all Singaporeans can benefit from it.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, CareShield Life cannot prevent us from falling sick.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: What is more important is that we exercise regularly, eat more healthy food.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
