text: The Minister has also said that MOH will work closely with grassroots organisations so that they can explain how ElderShield policyholders can convert to CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, to encourage those who have not participated in ElderShield to join CareShield is even more important.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In particular, we should encourage those low-income Singaporeans to join the scheme.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The subsidies can be lowered gradually each year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I will talk about the next two "small" questions in English.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, CareShield is a very good initiative, a very good insurance scheme and a very important social safety net.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: With this universal insurance scheme, I am concerned that it may overlap with other insurance policies that Singaporeans have been buying.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Some of these insurance policies come with disability income payouts.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: My understanding is that in the event of disability, people can only claim from one insurer unless the Government intervenes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We do not want a case whereby Singaporeans are over insured and paying insurance premiums more than necessary.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, I hope that MOH can coordinate with the insurance companies to prevent such an occurrence.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Last but not least, many Singaporeans would like to rehabilitate at home with tender loving care by their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, the caregivers at home face mounting challenges.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Even with CareShield, I hope the Government will continue to invest in resources to bring the nurses, therapists and doctors to the homes to help Singaporeans recover after a mishap.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe the CareShield Life Review Committee has done its best to address a wide range of issues concerning Singaporeans and has produced a comprehensive report articulating the tradeoffs considered and making many good recommendations for the scheme, formerly known as ElderShield.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: CareShield Life and MediShield Life are similar in their philosophy and principles, in essence, to provide basic protection for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In my speech during the Parliamentary debate on MediShield Life in 2014, I had set out my arguments in support of the scheme, and I would like to rehash part of it today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In principle, our health is ours and each of us has the responsibility of taking care of ourselves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, we know in reality that relying on ourselves alone may not be sufficient, as care expenses are costly and not everyone has high earning power.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, some Singaporeans may be more unfortunate to be hit by serious or debilitating illnesses that require long-term care.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, there is a need for additional support from other sources.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Different countries adopt different ways of tackling this issue.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some completely socialise the cost, and fund care expenses through taxes.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But this can lead to escalating, and potentially unsustainable, public healthcare expenditure.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In some developed economies like the United Kingdom (UK), public healthcare expenditure is one of the most costly fiscal items each year.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Others do it through insurance: collecting premiums from everyone, pooling the funds collected and then allocating the money as required by the population.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But such systems work only when everyone contributes, regardless of whether they think they will need to tap on the common pool.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This requires a strong sense of national solidarity and willingness to help their fellow countrymen.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In Singapore, we face similar challenges and responded with the 3M system, namely, MediSave, MediShield Life, and MediFund.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While the 3M framework is robust, this House agreed that we could do more as a society.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our society has been expounding the need to be caring and inclusive.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We all feel a deep sense of compassion when we see someone in pain and we all feel the need to help that someone to lead a life as normal as possible again.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As a society, we talked about it, we argued for it and we did it when this House finally passed the Bill on MediShield Life in 2014.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Through a universal public health insurance in the form of MediShield Life, we pooled our risks and money to help those who incur such expenses.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, we collectively understand the philosophy and need for public insurance as one of the pillars in our social safety net.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Since this House had supported MediShield Life, then, philosophically, there is no reason not to support CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, there are some questions and concerns that ordinary Singaporeans have and I would like to reflect these in this debate and to seek answers from the Government.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The first pertains to the New Enrolment batch, and that would be the young today.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This means that if we are lucky to live beyond 65 years, each of us has a 50% chance of becoming severely disabled in the remaining years and can expect to incur high cost of care in the years that follow.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Despite this high probability, our young today question the need for the scheme to be made mandatory for all.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many, who are still in the prime health, do not anticipate severe disabilities when they age.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Many also do not see the urgency in planning for the possibility of age-related disabilities at this point.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, they would want to preserve their autonomy in choosing whether and when to enrol themselves in such a universal public insurance scheme.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, there is a need for more and targeted engagements with the younger Singaporeans to not only explain the philosophy and design principles of CareShield Life, but to also answer the questions they have.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some of the questions would be as follows.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, for each cohort of Singaporeans, in terms of caring for an individual with disability, how much of the cost is borne by the Government, by the individual and by peers?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, what is the long-term financial impact on the system and on our population if Singaporeans preserve their right to choose whether to enrol in CareShield Life?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, could the Ministry explain why there remains such a huge sum of money in the pool?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fourth, looking ahead, for each cohort of premiums collected, what is the expected proportion of claims?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fifth, if there is money remaining from that cohort, what will happen to the money?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is a very real way of translating the idea of inclusivity into real policy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: However, the mandatory nature of the scheme also means we must garner overwhelming buy-in and support from Singaporeans in order to sustain this pillar of support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, we had a heated debate on MediShield Life in this House and passed the Bill in 2014.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Back then, the purpose of passing this medical insurance was to provide universal coverage for Singaporeans so that all will receive basic protection.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Besides Government grant and our own MediSave, MediShield Life will help us to cope with unforeseeable risks.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is a risk-pooling mechanism whereby people put their money together and allow those in need to pay for large medical bills.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Nowadays, our population is ageing rapidly and the family size is also shrinking.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is inevitable that Singaporeans must help one another and work together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, the implementation of MediShield Life is, in fact, to plan for our own, as well as for others' future.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In principle, CareShield Life and MediShield Life are the same.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In other words, among an elderly couple, one of them will, at some point, develop severe disabilities due to degenerative diseases and become dependent.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This will have a big impact on their living expenses in the coming years.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, to prepare Singaporeans for the future challenge is a pressing task.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Although we can understand the rationale behind the CareShield Life in principle, the Government must understand how this will affect our people and give appropriate support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The group that will be affected the most will be the middle-income, middle-aged Singaporeans – the so-called "sandwich class".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This group of people have their young to feed, old to support and are also feeling the effects of ageing.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They are most concerned about the affordability of CareShield Life premiums.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They are not only concerned about the increase of the premiums, but also whether they have enough cash to pay for this inevitable cost item.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They also have to pay for MediShield Life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Now that CareShield Life will be added on top of all these, they are worried that they would not have enough money.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They have also heard that the claim process is tedious.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: If severe disabilities indeed happen, the tedious process will be like “adding frost to snow”.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, the Government must give enough support to this group of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Otherwise, even if they have the heart to support CareShield Life, they may not have the ability to do so.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I hope the Government can pay more attention to the sandwich class and help them more.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They may have some illnesses but are generally still healthy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: They may not appear to qualify for MediFund or ElderFund because of their income but, in reality, they are under heavy family financial burdens.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For this group of people, what kind of support and protection will be available from the Government?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe our ultimate goal is to ensure that every Singaporean will have basic long-term care protection.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, the Government must balance various considerations and look after the vulnerable during implementation.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Only by doing this, can we achieve the goal of CareShield Life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The main reason articulated was that women have a longer lifespan on average and risk being disabled for a longer period of time.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is also a common practice in other countries.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Arguably, however, the idea of a public insurance plan is to pool risks and resources to help one another.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: First, should women not be allowed to pay the same amount of premium as the men in their respective cohorts?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Moreover, many women sacrificed their prime years to stay home and care for their loved ones.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The years away from work mean they may have little or significantly less savings in their MediSave.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These women may also not come from well-to-do families who have little to contribute to their MediSave even if they wish to.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: So, I would like to ask: what will the Government do to help this group of Singaporean women cope with the inevitable cost burden?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What can they count on to ensure their own long-term care and protection without having to fear burdening their own families?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My sincere hope is that we will all enjoy good health, lead a full and fulfilling life and, rather than having to spend on our care needs, are able to spend on things that we enjoy.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But the reality is that we can never be sure of what will happen to us in the years to come.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is also unsustainable and unfortunate if we have to burden future generations – which is, by the way, shrinking because of our ageing population – to fund our own care needs.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In a society that expounds the importance of compassion and inclusion, all of us will need to contribute, in ways big or small, in one way or another.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Besides financing, we should also invest in aged care service capacity, enhance care quality, and build communities of care and a strong social support system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In particular, Dr Lily Neo and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked how the Government is improving the long-term care infrastructure to help severely disabled seniors age and receive good home care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have also grown our healthcare workforce by about 36% since 2011.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will continue to expand the range of home and community care options and pilot new models of care, such as the Integrated Home and Day Care (IHDC) packages rolled out in 2016, which help to provide frail seniors with home and day care services that cater to their unique needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Second, we will also invest in improving service quality.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have progressively raised care standards, such as introducing the Enhanced Nursing Home Standards (ENHS) to ensure residents receive safe and good care.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We have also introduced developmental service guidelines as a reference for home and centre-based providers to work towards delivering good quality care for our seniors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Third, we are integrating social and healthcare support to better meet the needs of our elderly in their communities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We are building communities of care through the Community Networks for Seniors (CNS) programme to help seniors age well in the community through preventive health and active ageing programmes and the integration of social and healthcare support for frail seniors with complex health and social needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: With the new Silver Generation Office (SGO) under AIC, MOH can better serve our seniors’ needs in a holistic manner, with support from over 3,000 Silver Generation Ambassadors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh suggested recruiting Ambassadors to explain the enhancements to residents.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will definitely leverage SGO’s outreach capabilities to reach out to seniors, explain how these new enhancements help support their long-term care needs and direct them to relevant financial assistance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Residents will find the Ambassadors a familiar face as they had also helped many seniors understand the PG Package, MedShield Life and many other assistance schemes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Fourth, the Government will continue to support the needs of Singaporeans with ageing-related cognitive conditions and their caregivers under the Community Mental Health Masterplan.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For instance, we have established six Dementia Friendly Communities to increase the awareness of dementia in these communities so that persons with dementia and their families feel included and supported to continue living at home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We aim to have 15 such Communities by 2021.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: While we continue to improve our service capacity and quality and grow community networks to better support our elderly, we must also ensure that Singaporeans plan ahead and are able to financially cope with their long-term care needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Minister Gan has outlined our long-term care financing philosophy and the role that insurance plays, together with family and Government support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The ESRC made many good recommendations, and I am optimistic that these enhancements will provide better protection and assurance for Singaporeans to age actively and well in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: First, the new CareShield Life will be an inclusive scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This means that all Singaporeans in these cohorts will have basic protection for their long-term care should they become severely disabled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, Ms Jessica Tan, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Ang Wei Neng have asked why CareShield Life is not optional for future cohorts, given that some young Singaporeans might already have bought their own policies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Including all future cohorts allows us to maximise the size of the risk pool, which keeps premiums affordable and the scheme sustainable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: If the scheme is optional, those with pre-existing disabilities cannot be covered, as healthy Singaporeans would be more likely to opt out of the scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Over time, the risk-pool would worsen and the scheme would become unsustainable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Other vulnerable groups like the low-income may also drop out of the scheme because of an inability to pay.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As CareShield Life provides payouts in cash, they would not duplicate existing policies that Singaporeans may already have purchased.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: There is also a misperception that private disability insurance products, such as total and permanent disability plans or disability income replacement plans, provide similar coverage to CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These plans typically only provide coverage during one's working years, up to age 60 to 70, as they are meant to insure against loss of income.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This means that in our old age, when we are most likely to become severely disabled and need long-term care, we will no longer be covered by these plans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: On the other hand, CareShield Life will provide coverage for life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: There are different views among Members about what age should Singaporeans be enrolled into CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh suggested 21, Mr Ang Wei Neng suggested 40.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The ESRC likewise received a range of suggestions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We agree with their recommendation to start at 30, and we understand that this was an age that many youths engaged by the Committee felt would be reasonable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: At 30, most feel that they would have started working and managed to build up some savings in their MediSave.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Starting at 30 instead of 40 also means they have more years to spread their premium payments, which makes their annual premiums more manageable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Government will provide means-tested premium subsidies and transitional subsidies to ensure that premiums are affordable, particularly for the lower-income.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will also provide Additional Premium Support for those who are unable to afford their premiums even after subsidies, so that no one loses coverage due to financial difficulties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Including those with pre-existing disabilities in future cohorts in our national long-term care insurance scheme is part of our collective responsibility and is fundamental to our inclusive and caring society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Individuals in future cohorts with any pre-existing disabilities will only need to pay the first-year premium to join CareShield Life, and, thereafter, will be able to benefit from the payouts, as long as they remain severely disabled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The premium amount is less than the first monthly CareShield Life payout they will receive.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: An individual who will benefit is 36-year-old Mr Mohamed Hasan, who has cerebral palsy and is physically unable to perform all ADLs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As he will be part of the future cohorts to be enrolled in 2020, he will be able to receive CareShield Life payouts from 2020 for as long as he remains severely disabled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked how many Singaporeans in the future cohorts have severe disability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The prevalence of severe disability at younger ages is low.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Only a very small proportion, less than 0.1%, of the future cohorts aged 30 to 40 may already be severely disabled when they first join CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The remainder of the costs will be socialised across all CareShield Life policyholders in the future cohorts, with everyone playing our part to support fellow Singaporeans in need.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is in line with our vision of an inclusive and caring society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: During public consultations, the ESRC also found support for this among Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi and Mr Zainal Sapari asked why CareShield Life is not universal and mandatory for Singaporeans from existing cohorts, since CareShield Life provides better protection and greater assurance than ElderShield.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Committee had considered this during their review, and decided this was not feasible, given the nature of CareShield Life as a prefunded insurance scheme.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Unlike MediShield Life where premiums are paid for life, CareShield Life premiums are paid till age 67 even though it provides lifetime coverage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This means that CareShield Life premiums are heavily prefunded.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Older Singaporeans from the existing cohorts would, therefore, need to pay significantly higher annual premiums under CareShield Life, as they would have fewer years to spread out their premiums needed to support the benefits under CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Some Singaporeans in existing cohorts have also previously made decisions about their ElderShield coverage when they were auto-enrolled at age 40, as Mr Png Eng Huat had also shared earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Others may also have made plans for their long-term care needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: As of 2017, about one-third of ElderShield policyholders have bought ElderShield Supplements from the ElderShield insurers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Taking into account these considerations, the Committee recommended that it would not be practical to make CareShield Life mandatory for these individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: However, the scheme should remain open for them to join, if they are not already severely disabled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I want to assure Members that CareShield Life will still be an inclusive scheme for existing cohorts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong asked about the treatment for Singaporeans in existing cohorts who want to join CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Singaporeans in existing cohorts can join the scheme as long as they are not severely disabled or able to perform at least three ADLs, even if they have medical conditions, such as diabetes or hypertension.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is consistent with our inclusive vision for CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These incentives will help to shoulder a significant part of the costs of including those in the existing cohorts with pre-existing medical conditions or mild disabilities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is on top of the premium subsidies we are providing to lower- and middle-income policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: After the first two years, underwriting will be tightened such that those in the existing cohorts assessed to be unable to do any of the ADLs will not be able to join to minimise adverse selection and moral hazard so that the scheme remains sustainable and fair for all policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For ElderShield policyholders who do not wish to join CareShield Life, they will continue to be protected by their current ElderShield policies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Dr Lily Neo and Ms K Thanaletchimi asked how would those who are already severely disabled in the existing cohorts be helped, if they are unable to join CareShield Life?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah also asked for the actuarial considerations and premium impact, if we were to include those with pre-existing severe disabilities in the existing cohorts from CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: These are initiatives that Minister Gan spoke about earlier.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked whether the payout amounts for these new initiatives are enough.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Nevertheless, Ms Thanaletchimi, Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Ms Tin Pei Ling should rest assured that the Government will continue to review our financing policies to keep healthcare and long-term care affordable for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Many members, like Dr Chia Shi-Lu, Ms Sylvia Lim, Assoc Prof Daniel Goh, Mr Melvin Yong and Ms Tin Pei Ling, have also asked why CareShield Life premiums have to be gender differentiated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The ESRC had debated this topic extensively and it was not an easy decision to make.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Women live longer than men and are, therefore, more likely to spend more years in severe disability, as all of us are more likely to become severely disabled at the older ages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In 2017, the average life expectancy at birth for women is 85.2 years, as compared to 80.7 years for men.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Minister Gan had earlier shared that one in two Singaporeans at the age of 65 are expected to become severely disabled by the end of their lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Breaking this down by gender, using the same statistics, three in five healthy women at age 65 are expected to become severely disabled by the end of their lives, compared to two in five healthy men at age 65.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: At the older ages, when disability is likely to take place, women are also more likely to remain in disability for a longer time than men and, hence, will draw on CareShield Life payouts for a longer period should they become severely disabled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Based on a longitudinal survey of older Singaporeans in 2009 and 2011 to 2012, researchers estimated women aged 60 are expected to spend 7.8 years requiring assistance with any of the ADLs by the end of their lives, compared to 2.6 years for men aged 60.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Other countries, like the US, found similar gender-differentiated disability trends.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In a longitudinal study of US men and women between 1982 and 2011, researchers estimated women aged 65 in 2011 are expected to spend about six years requiring assistance with ADLs by the end of their lives, compared to about three-and-a-half years for men aged 65 in 2011.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Two-thirds of long-term insurance claims benefits paid out in 2012 went towards females.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: It is, of course, possible to have a scheme where men and women pay the same premiums.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: While CareShield Life is compulsory for future cohorts, it must be noted that it is not compulsory for existing cohorts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Hence, it is better to be actuarially fair and correct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Committee emphasised, however, the need to provide premium support for lower-income and middle-income policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Government accepts the Committee’s recommendations, though I must assure this House that the Ministry, not just myself, but my other colleagues, similarly had great difficulty in coming to this decision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Some may ask why should we differentiate premiums between men and women if we say CareShield Life is an inclusive scheme?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: While we have designed CareShield Life to be inclusive, on balance, it is also important for the scheme to be equitable and sustainable and avoid adverse selection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: To that end, premiums must be actuarially sound.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Government will address the issue of affordability directly.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In line with the progressive design of our healthcare financing system, the Government's premium subsidies for CareShield Life are means-tested, with the quantum of support based on a percentage of premiums.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This also means lower- and middle-income females will receive larger dollar quantum of Government subsidies, compared to the men in their age cohort with the same income levels.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: And in line with our effort to promote strong family values, care and support, immediate family members, such as their spouse, can also help pay for their premiums with their MediSave, or top-up their MediSave with cash to help them pay for the premiums.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Government will also provide Additional Premium Support for those with less financial means, so that no one will lose coverage due to financial difficulties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Overall, this design will support the sustainability of CareShield Life, while ensuring that premiums remain affordable for all Singaporeans, regardless of gender.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will continue to explore how to give more help to women who face difficulties but, on balance, it is more prudent to keep the scheme actuarially correct and fair.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Some will ask why this is a different approach from MediShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: MediShield Life premiums are payable for as long as a policyholder lives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: While women may make more claims since they live longer, they would also have paid more years of MediShield Life premiums compared to men.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Second, CareShield Life provides flexibility to age in place.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: In enhancing our long-term care financing system, it is also important to bear in mind that Singaporeans have different needs and preferences for their long-term care, and the majority prefer to age at home and in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Similar to ElderShield, the Committee had recommended CareShield Life to provide cash payouts instead of using CareShield Life to reimburse the use of specific long-term care services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Reimbursement of specific long-term care services may, at first glance, provide more reassurance to claimants and their caregivers, as the reimbursements would be pegged to the costs of the services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: However, cash payouts will provide claimants and their caregivers more flexibility to decide on care arrangements appropriate to their needs and do not limit care to certain long-term care services in order to be eligible for claim.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This design also recognises that long-term care needs might extend beyond medical needs and will better support policyholders who choose informal care at home or in the community instead of formal care services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Cash payouts also support our overall efforts to go Beyond Hospital To Community, to support care in the community and allow more seniors to be cared for at home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Government also currently provides subsidies of up to 80% for home and community care services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This is also why we designed the two new enhancements that Minister Gan announced – MediSave withdrawals for long-term care and ElderFund – to also pay out in cash.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked what safeguards will be put in place to ensure cash payouts will be spent on the care of severely disabled individuals, especially those suffering from dementia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We recognise that severely disabled individuals may be more susceptible to exploitation, especially if they lose mental capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will design the three schemes’ claims processes carefully, and put in place checks and audits to ensure that payouts are used for the care needs of the claimant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We will do this in a way that does not inconvenience the claimant or his caregivers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: It is also useful for all of us to make a Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) early and choose our donee carefully, as Ms K Thanaletchimi pointed out.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We should appoint someone we trust to act in our best interests should we lose the capacity to make decisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Some of these policyholders and their families or care providers have provided feedback that the current ElderShield claims process is confusing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked how we will ensure that severely disabled policyholders and their caregivers navigate the claims process more easily.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: We wholeheartedly support the recommendations by the Committee to improve the claims process for CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: The Committee had put in a lot of effort to understand the current ElderShield claims process and developed a good set of recommendations to improve the claims process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Under CareShield Life, policyholders and their caregivers can expect a claims process that is easier to navigate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For CareShield Life, we will not require policyholders to arrange for a separate disability assessment, if an equivalent disability assessment had already been done for them by their doctor, therapist or nurse in the course of receiving care in a health or long-term care setting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For those who need a separate disability assessment, we will expand the pool of assessors beyond doctors to include occupational therapists, physiotherapists and nurses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: This will make it more convenient to go for an assessment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi suggested the assessment fee be waived for the cognitively impaired.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Subsequent assessment fees will be reimbursed if the claim is successful.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms Joan Pereira’s suggestion for proper communication to policyholders who make a recovery is also well-noted, and we will certainly follow through on it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi and Mr Murali Pillai asked how we can help seniors who are cognitively impaired, for instance, with dementia, benefit from CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: I want to, first, clarify that those with cognitive impairments and are unable to perform three or more ADLs are already able to benefit from ElderShield today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Under today’s assessment framework, assessors are already supposed to take into account how cognitive impairments impact the policyholder’s ability to perform the ADLs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Many policyholders with severe dementia are already able to make ElderShield claims today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: One policyholder who benefited from ElderShield is 77-year-old Mdm Leong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: Although Mdm Leong is physically able to eat and walk, she is unable to recall the way to specific places, such as the toilet, or express her needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Dr Amy Khor Lean Suan)
text: For instance, in the current assessment framework, the assessor may only evaluate solely whether a policyholder with severe dementia can execute the physical actions, such as threading their arms through sleeves.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Let us hold the clarifications until the end.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I would also want to join Members in expressing my appreciation to the ESRC led by Mr Chaly Mah, and the Secretariat Team from MOH.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Committee’s recommendations on the new CareShield Life scheme are significant measures to enhance Singapore’s long-term care financing and provide a stronger social safety net with our ageing population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Through risk-pooling, CareShield Life will enhance the role of insurance in helping Singaporeans meet our long-term care needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It will add to the other sources of funding for long-term care, including Government subsidies, personal savings and family support, and financial assistance for the lower-income.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I will touch on a few issues in my speech: first, how the features of CareShield Life provide better protection and greater assurance for Singaporeans; second, how the scheme is designed to meet basic long-term care needs while remaining affordable; third, what are the support measures for existing cohorts to join CareShield Life; fourth, how the scheme can remain sustainable for the longer term; and finally, the Government’s plans to explain the scheme and raise public awareness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: ESRC had engaged a large group of Singaporeans over the course of its work and received many useful feedback and suggestions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Committee had to decide which enhancements are most important and how to balance the improvements in benefits with the need to keep premiums affordable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If the benefits are not adequate, the scheme would not provide sufficient protection.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: On the other hand, if the benefits are very generous, premiums may become too high.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We need to strike a balance, as Mr Christopher de Souza had eloquently explained.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We agree with the Committee that CareShield Life payouts should be provided for life, to give policyholders and their family better peace of mind.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In addition, CareShield Life payouts will increase gradually over time to keep pace with inflation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These features will offer better protection for policyholders, compared to ElderShield, which pays a flat rate of $300 or $400 per month.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is three times the current amount of payouts under ElderShield 400.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This policyholder will receive monthly payouts of $1,200 for life if he remains severely disabled, until he passes away.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Next, I will explain how CareShield Life is designed to meet basic long-term care needs while remaining affordable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Lily Neo, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Christopher de Souza asked whether $600 per month will be enough, and if payout increases can continue for life even after a claim has been made.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Several Members also asked whether the criterion can be relaxed so that those who are unable to perform at least two ADLs could receive payouts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We understand the rationale for these suggestions, which is to provide more benefits to policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Committee has also discussed these ideas and carefully considered the tradeoffs of further increasing the payout amount and lowering the claims criterion, versus the need to keep premiums affordable in a universal insurance scheme that caters to a broad segment of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If we allow the payout amount to continue increasing for life after a claim is made, premiums would have to increase further, possibly by another one-third.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari and Ms Joan Pereira also asked if premium discounts could be given to ElderShield or CareShield Life policyholders who do not make claims, to incentivise healthy living.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: ElderShield and CareShield Life, being prefunded schemes, policyholders would pay premiums when they are young and receive coverage for life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Hence, one can only confirm that a policyholder is not claiming from the scheme after the policyholder has passed away.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In computing the premiums, the actuaries have included the probability that some policyholders will not claim from the scheme because they do not become severely disabled.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In other words, this has already been incorporated in the premium quantum.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: In view of the tradeoffs, the Committee recommended that CareShield Life focuses on supporting basic long-term care needs so that premiums can be kept affordable for all groups of policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Dr Lily Neo and Ms Joan Pereira asked if Singaporeans who wish to have more benefits, such as coverage for less severe disability or higher payouts, and are willing to pay higher premiums, will they be able to purchase additional coverage from private insurers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Currently, ElderShield policyholders can use up to $600 per year from their MediSave to pay for ElderShield Supplement premiums.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOH will work with private insurers to adapt the design of their Supplements to complement CareShield Life and continue to allow policyholders to use MediSave to pay for these Supplements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: It is also important to remember that CareShield Life payouts are not the only source of long-term care financing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They will complement other financing sources, such as Government subsidies and assistance schemes, personal savings and family support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Singaporeans with mild or moderate disabilities and who need long-term care can tap on means-tested Government subsidies for nursing home, community care and homecare.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are also other Government schemes, such as the Seniors’ Mobility and Enabling Fund, PG Disability Assistance Scheme and the Foreign Domestic Worker Grant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: But if he receives $600 per month from CareShield Life and utilises $200 from his MediSave account under the new MediSave withdrawal scheme, he and his family would need to pay around $200 per month from their savings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: If this person chooses home and day care services under the Integrated Home and Day Care pilot programme, he can reduce his out-of-pocket expenses to almost zero through a combination of Government subsidies, CareShield Life payouts and MediSave withdrawals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And that is why we have introduced the new ElderFund scheme, to provide further protection for these vulnerable groups of Singaporeans for their long-term care needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: ElderFund will add to the protection offered under existing assistance schemes like MediFund and ComCare.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked how the Government will further support Singaporeans, including the self-employed or unemployed, in paying their premiums.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked why this AV threshold was used.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This threshold covers about 80% of properties in Singapore, including all HDB flats and some private properties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We used a similar set of means-testing criteria for MediShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And about two in three Singaporeans will be eligible for the subsidies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Individuals who do not meet the means-testing criteria, but face genuine financial difficulties in paying their premiums, can apply for Additional Premium Support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Their application will be considered on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The budget for Additional Premium Support is fully funded by the Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This will help to further reduce the premium amounts for these policyholders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked why the transitional subsidies are provided only for the first five years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: These subsidies aim to ease transition into CareShield Life for the immediate few future cohorts who will be joining the scheme from 2020.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And these are the cohorts from age 30 to 40 in 2020 as well as those turning 30 between 2021 and 2024.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Compared to the subsequent cohorts who will join the scheme later, they have less time to prepare for the higher premiums under CareShield Life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The transitional subsidies are intended to cushion the impact for these few cohorts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The amount of subsidies will be gradually reduced over the five-year period.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: CareShield Life is part of our social safety net and we will ensure that no Singaporean will lose coverage due to financial difficulties and inability to pay premiums.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: They do not need to make additional cash payouts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Education and Trade and Industry (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: And, with your permission, Mr Deputy Speaker, may I display a slide?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Here, we have a family where the husband and wife, Mr and Mrs Koh, are both aged 40 and each person is earning $2,200 per month.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But as Ms Jessica Tan said, MediSave is also needed for other healthcare-related expenses and that is why we have to keep a balance between the benefits and the premium quantum for CareShield Life, while allowing policyholders to purchase Supplements if they wish to do so.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I will now move on to describe the support measures for existing cohorts to join CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor had earlier explained why we decided not to make CareShield Life mandatory for Singaporeans in the existing cohorts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We do want to encourage as many Singaporeans as possible to join the scheme if they are not already severely disabled, so that more Singaporeans can pool our risks together and have better protection and greater peace of mind for everyone as we age.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Zainal Sapari asked if the Government will support those who convert from ElderShield to CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will also provide means-tested subsidies and Additional Premium Support under CareShield Life to policyholders from the existing cohort to ensure no one loses coverage due to financial difficulties.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These are the younger members of the existing cohorts who are currently on ElderShield 400.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Compared to older members of the existing cohorts and those who are not on ElderShield 400, the quantum of their premiums to join CareShield Life will be lower.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The purpose of auto-enrolment is to make it more convenient for this group of Singaporeans to join CareShield Life, and policyholders will automatically receive the premium subsidies and participation incentives.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: They will be given at least two years, up to 31 December 2023, to opt out of CareShield Life if they do not wish to join the scheme.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Auto-enrolment is to make it more convenient, but it remains optional for them.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Older members in existing cohorts who are born in 1969 or earlier, including those who have previously opted out of ElderShield, can also join CareShield Life if they are not already severely disabled.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will support them if they wish to join the scheme.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And unlike ElderShield, there is no age limit to join CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: MOH will make a premium calculator available by the end of this year for existing cohorts to find out more details about their premiums.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We encourage Singaporeans who are interested to join CareShield Life to take their time to understand more about the scheme and how it can meet their long-term care needs before deciding.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is no hurry, as the sign-up period only starts in 2021 for existing cohorts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Minister Gan had explained how long-term care insurance schemes like ElderShield and CareShield Life are prefunded to ensure long-term sustainability.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In designing the scheme, we want to ensure that premiums paid by each generation during their working years can support their future claims when they grow old.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This minimises intergenerational transfers, so that as our population ages and our families get smaller, claims made by the older generation can be met without having the younger generation shoulder a heavier financial burden.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is an important part of ensuring long-term sustainability, especially when we are facing an ageing society.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Pritam Singh touched on this in his speech, too.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Leon Perera and Mr Png Eng Huat also asked how premiums are determined.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In prefunded insurance schemes like ElderShield and CareShield Life, premiums are collected when the policyholders are younger and working, so that the fund has enough resources to meet their future claims when they grow old and are no longer paying premiums.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As Senior Minister of State Amy Khor mentioned earlier, the coverage is for life.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is, therefore, logical and necessary for the scheme to show a positive balance when policyholders are younger and are less likely to be severely disabled.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This also answers Dr Lily Neo’s question on why the number of claimants is currently low.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: ElderShield policyholders are still relatively young, with a median age of 52 in 2017.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: However, as policyholders grow older and more of them become severely disabled, the balance amount that we see today will be gradually used up to pay for claims.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This balance amount is not profit, it is to meet future liabilities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: If a prefunded scheme does not have a positive balance when its policyholders are younger, the scheme is actually in trouble.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It means there will not be enough financial resources to meet future liabilities, and when policyholders grow older and more of them start to claim, the scheme will have difficulties making the payouts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The balance amounts for ElderShield that are currently with the three private insurers will be properly accounted for.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We are working on this with the insurers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this is based on a mix of local and international data sources.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For example, in 2016, the US Department of Health and Human Services estimated that 52% Americans turning 65 in 2016 would develop a disability serious enough to require long-term care.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: It is important to remember that the premium calculations are based on a complex actuarial model with many factors, and not just on one number.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I do not intend to go through the technical details of the actuarial model in this House.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But let me say that a premium pricing model was done by professional actuaries, in line with internationally-accepted industry standards.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Some factors that they incorporated in their model include the disabled mortality rate, recovery rate, claims continuance rate, mortality rate, improvements to mortality rate, disability incidence, prevalence rate, as well as the risk profile for various cohorts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In addition, premiums for the existing cohorts will need to take into account their circumstances, for example, some are on ElderShield 300, some are on ElderShield 400 and some are not insured at all.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will discuss with the council and the actuaries on how best to share information on the details and assumptions for CareShield Life meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: ElderShield policyholders will be no worse off and will continue to be covered by these insurance schemes.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government will set up an independent council by legislation, comprising people with various expertise and background.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We agree with Ms Joan Pereira that the council should consider views from social workers, healthcare professionals and insurance experts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The council will regularly review and recommend changes in premiums and payouts, guided by professional advice from independent actuaries, and decide on the optimal investment strategy of the fund.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: AIC, which has experience in implementing disability schemes, will work with CPF Board, which has experience in managing insurance schemes, to administer CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: CPF Board will also be the administrator of the CareShield Life Fund and will ensure that the funds are safeguarded for the benefit of policyholders.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The annual financial statements will be made publicly available.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Mr Ang Wei Neng asked how premiums and payouts will be adjusted.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We envision the adjustment framework to work like this: if claims are lower than the amount assumed in the actuarial modelling and calculations, the CareShield Life council could recommend higher payout increases or provide policyholders with premium rebates in subsequent years.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Conversely, if claims are higher than what was originally assumed in the actuarial modelling and calculations, the council could recommend raising premiums or slowing down payout increases to ensure the scheme remains sustainable.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government will invest the funds prudently to earn stable returns.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But what is not possible to predict with full accuracy are factors, such as the frequency and duration of claims.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Singaporeans who join the scheme now and start to contribute in their working years must have assurance that should they become severely disabled when they are old, there will be enough funds to draw upon for their long-term care needs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In addition, we want to ensure that future generations will not be burdened with the cost of financing our long-term care needs when we grow old.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Over the past week, since we announced further details on CareShield Life, we have heard feedback that the scheme can be rather complicated, and many Singaporeans find it challenging to understand all the details.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This feedback has also been raised by several Members today.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There is still some time before CareShield Life takes effect in 2020 for future cohorts, and 2021 for existing cohorts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will use this period to reach out to different groups of Singaporeans and explain to everyone the details of the scheme and how it can meet their long-term care needs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will intensify our public education efforts on the risks of severe disability in old age, and what are the available long-term care financing sources that can complement CareShield Life to support the long-term care needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These include Government subsidies for nursing home, community care and home care services, assistance schemes like ElderFund, as well as the use of personal savings like MediSave withdrawals for long-term care.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: MOH will step up our outreach and engagement efforts through mainstream and social media.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will also partner the grassroots, Silver Generation ambassadors, youth and union leaders, financial advisors, and other Government agencies, such as the People’s Association (PA), CPF Board and the Monetary Authority of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: (In Mandarin):   CareShield Life will provide Singaporeans with better protection for their basic long-term care needs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Upon becoming severely disabled, policyholders will be able to receive lifetime payouts, to support their long-term care cost, until recovery or death.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are various long-term care financing sources, such as Government subsidies and assistance schemes, personal and family savings and community support.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The payouts under CareShield Life will complement these financing sources to support Singaporeans with their basic long-term care needs.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government will also provide support to help policyholders with their CareShield Life premiums.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Additional premium support will also be available to Singaporeans who cannot afford their premiums even after the subsidies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For those born in 1979 or earlier and who are not already severely disabled, they can opt to join the scheme in 2021.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We will make sure that all Singaporeans who join CareShield Life will not lose coverage due to inability to afford premiums.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Singaporeans can also tap on two new schemes to support their long-term care cost.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government is also setting up a new ElderFund scheme to provide up to $250 per month for low-income citizens with severe disabilities.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As our society ages, CareShield Life and other related schemes will strengthen our social safety net.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: These will provide Singaporeans with better protection and greater peace of mind for our long-term care needs when we grow old.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: (In English): The introduction of CareShield Life will provide better protection and assurance for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: All future cohorts of Singaporeans will have sustainable, basic protection for their long-term care needs through CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This includes vulnerable groups like low-income families and those who are already severely disabled.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Through a universal risk-pooling scheme like CareShield Life, we can offer coverage for everyone in the future cohorts.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We also want to encourage Singaporeans from the existing cohorts to join the scheme.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Under CareShield Life, the Government will provide Singaporeans with premium subsidies and financial support so that no one will lose coverage if they face financial difficulties and are unable to pay their premiums.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: For those who are not able to join CareShield Life, the Government will help them through other schemes, such as the MediSave withdrawal for long-term care and ElderFund.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: As our society grows older, some of us will become severely disabled and require long-term care.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: We have to take steps to prepare for this ahead of time when we are still young and healthy.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is what we want to achieve with long-term care insurance schemes like CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Together with Government subsidies, personal savings and family support, CareShield Life will further strengthen our social safety net and provide Singaporeans with better protection and greater assurance when we grow old.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Young Singaporeans typically think about long-term care as something that is not important and not on their radar scan.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In fact, many of them regard such issues as issues for the old.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: That is why it is important for us to address this issue now.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Very often, we only realise how important these issues are when we have to take care of someone who is severely disabled – our family members.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: As Dr Chia Shi-Lu’s grandmother’s experience has shown, often, this happens very suddenly, and we are not prepared for it because we never planned for this.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Therefore, today, I am happy that we have this opportunity in this House to talk about CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I am encouraged that Members of this House have voiced support for the introduction of CareShield Life to provide better protection and greater assurance, compared to the current ElderShield.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Members have also made very thoughtful remarks and suggestions and shared concerns which Singaporeans might have.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Some of these relate to the design of the scheme: whom it should cover; its benefits, features; and how it will be managed.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: There were also questions about the affordability, and concerns about how Singaporeans without CareShield Life, or those who need additional help, can be supported.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Senior Ministers of State Amy Khor and Chee Hong Tat have addressed most of the concerns and questions raised.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Allow me now to sum up the debate on long-term care and CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: First, CareShield Life will be an inclusive scheme.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We have explained why it is not possible to make it mandatory for all Singaporeans in the existing cohorts – those born in 1979 or earlier – to join CareShield Life.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will, however, encourage them to do so, with participation incentives.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In line with our inclusive principle, those with pre-existing conditions but are not severely disabled will also be allowed to join the scheme.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: On affordability, some Members of the House have raised concerns about what will happen if there are people who may not be able to afford their premiums.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: These include the self-employed, housewives and the low-income.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: In other words, the financially needy will receive additional support from the Government on their premiums.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Making sure that CareShield Life premiums remain affordable also requires a delicate balance between better benefits and their impact on premiums.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: While these suggestions are well-intended, we have to balance these enhancements against premium affordability as they will lead to higher premiums.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We also should bear in mind that insurance payouts are not the only source of long-term care funding.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Personal and family savings, other Government subsidies and safety nets and community support also play a role.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: This is the reason why the ESRC recommended that CareShield Life should provide a basic level of protection for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Those who prefer additional insurance cover have the option to buy Supplements from private insurers using their MediSave savings, according to their individual preferences and financial resources.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: That said, ensuring that CareShield Life remains affordable is just one part of the larger picture.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I agree with Dr Chia Shi-Lu, Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Chen Show Mao that we do need to pay attention to maintaining and managing long-term care costs.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: We will continue to do our best to work with all our stakeholders to better manage our long-term care cost, but all of us will also have a role to play to stay healthy and prevent ourselves from falling into disability.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Third, let me emphasise that CareShield Life, being a vital part of our future social safety net, must be sustainable for generations to come.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: The scheme is not intended for younger generations to cross-subsidise the older generations.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: Other countries have found such pay-as-you-go systems difficult to sustain.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To be sustainable, premiums must also be priced according to sound actuarial principles.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: To ensure this, an independent Council will be established through legislation to advise the Government on premium and payout adjustments.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: I would also like to emphasise again that the Government will administer CareShield Life on a not-for-profit basis.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
text: All premiums collected will go into the CareShield Life Fund of policyholders.

speaker: Mr Gan Kim Yong
